subsubtopic: PROVISION AFFECTING CORPORATE-OWNED LIFE INSURANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The retention of our small private businesses and their orderly transfer to the next generation on the deaths of their owners are in the interest of the Canadian economy, rather than their forced sale to large corporate interests, often foreign-owned. However, the rollovers contained in the Income Tax Act to permit a tax-free transfer to the next generation are very limited, except in the case of farmers. Corporately owned life insurance used in conjunction with an appropriate buy-sell arrangement previously permitted a mechanism to effect a transfer without tax to the next generation. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn):
That the Minister of Finance reverse the Government's position, so that proceeds of corporate-owned life insurance purchased after June 28 be no longer credited to a company's capital dividend account.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATE OF PREPAREDNESS OF THRONE SPEECH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was ready some time in mid October. We had envisaged the possibility of having the Throne Speech read at the end of the month of October. There was a speech ready. It can be made ready at any time. The House Leader attempted, in discussions with his opposite numbers, to see whether we would be able to make progress before the Christmas adjournment on the very important legislation which was already before the House in this session, particularly those measures relating to the last budget and the budget before.
The Leader of the Opposition knows, if he is being kept informed by his House Leader, that for the past two weeks now we have been attempting to get some agreement on a package of legislative measures which we would be able to
clear away before reading the Throne Speech. I understand that there is no agreement on the package but that there has been progress on individual bills, several of which have been processed through the House.
It is still our hope that we will be able to deal with the backlog of measures arising from two or three budgets removed, before reading the Speech from the Throne. That does not mean that we have not acted on some of the measures which would have been announced in that Speech from the Throne.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what the Prime Minister or his colleague has been busy negotiating over the last little while is to try to get agreement in the Liberal Party on how they will vote on Bill C-133 and how they will vote on Canagrex. That is what he has been trying to negotiate over the last little while.
Hear, hear!

Let me return to what this Government will do to help Canadians who are suffering because of Liberal economic policy. The Prime Minister has promised that there will be bold and innovative action on the economy in the Throne Speech. His House Leader says that the Throne Speech is ready. Why does the Government wait for the Throne Speech to begin action to solve the economic problems of the country? Why will he not bring in economic action now to help the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are in need and who are losing hope with each passing day?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition misses the point. The Throne Speech was ready. In view of the fact we did not begin the session with the Throne Speech, but, rather, postponed it, as I say, until we deal with this legislative backlog, we announced those measures, some by the Minister of Finance in his statement at the beginning of this part of the session. Another announcement which was to be in the Throne Speech was concerning the Royal Commission.
Oh, oh!

These are examples of measures taken, including one involving $1,100 million, which would have been in the Throne Speech had we proceeded with the Throne Speech. Therefore, the Leader of the Opposition really must be making great efforts not to grasp, but the instrument through which the announcements were made is secondary. The important thing is that the Government has been making announcements. It has been taking bold, innovative measures in order to deal with unemployment.


November 18, 1982

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. 1 remind the Minister that in his statement on basic economic principles of management, he said on October 27, "We must continue to rely firmly on the dynamism and the creativity of the private sector as the engine of growth in Canada".
Hear, hear!

Well, I am glad you are clapping, Doug.
He went on to say that we must improve the financial health of the private sector as well as its ability to expand and prosper. Since that time the only actions we have seen have been the allotment of $400 million to losing Crown corporations and $600 million to buy some service stations, and a further tax of $1.7 billion on employment. What further efforts have there been by the Minister of Finance to improve the health, dynamism and activity of the private sector?

Madam Speaker, it is typical of those in the Conservative Party, I am afraid, that they would rather have a company owned by the British Government than owned by the people of Canada through their Government.
Hear, hear!

However, putting that aside, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that, in the statement 1 made, I announced expenditures of $1.1 billion which will be directed toward job creation. 1 indicated that $400 million will be concentrated upon improvement of the railway system in western Canada. That will have a very significant impact on the private sector in terms of additional orders in the manufacturing sector all across Canada.
Quid pro quo.

In addition to the $500 million under the NEED Program, we have indicated that those funds would also be available to projects which could be sponsored in the private sector. Moreover, in my statement I announced a number of measures which were of a tax relieving nature to various sectors, small business in particular, which have made representations for relieving measures. All those measures are on the record and I would be very pleased to send a copy of my October 27 statement to the Hon. Member.
The Minister will know that the cost to Canadians amounts to 47,000 person-years of employment because of his increase in unemployment insurance premiums alone. So much for his work-creating efforts.

1 direct my supplementary question to the same Minister. Interest rates seem to

Now we have a positive balance of payments at this point. Now, unfortunately, interest rates seem to be going up in the United States.

The first one having to do with the loss of jobs created by the increase in the unemployment insurance contributions is completely unsubstantiated and I challenge him to prove those figures. I am surprised that my hon. friend is expressing so much concern when I did not hear him mention the issue, for 14 weeks in a row, until this week, when we have had a significant decline in interest rates in Canada.

speechtext:

Considering that the Minister yesterday, before a Senate Committee, made the extraordinary assertion that Bill S-31 was necessary to stop the Caisse from creating socialism, I would like to ask him what does he mean by this when the Caisse cannot have more than 30 per cent of the shares in an enterprise on the one hand, and, secondly, what business is it of the federal Government to stop any duly elected provincial Government in Canada from creating as many public enterprises as it wants.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: EFFECT ON INVESTMENT OF QUEBEC PENSION FUNDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 may comment that the Hon. Member's question was preceded by a very long preamble, and that the Hon. Member is a little mixed up. Once more, and it would be useful if the Hon. Member would understand this, Bill S-31 is aimed at safeguarding federal jurisdiction over interprovincial and international transport. The purpose of the bill is not to prevent an institution such as the Caisse de depot or other financial institutions in Canada from investing. On the contrary, they are welcome to do so. They may invest, but these provincial institutions may not own more than 10 per cent of the shares.
In many cases, Madam Speaker, 10 per cent is a great deal, and we should also remember that the financial institution referred to by the Leader of the New Democratic Party was created for the purpose of managing funds and not with a view to taking risks and becoming an active shareholder. I think that by its actions and recent statements, the Caisse has clearly shown that it is going beyond the judicious investment of Quebec's pension fund and that it has now become a company that is taking risks and playing the market with the pension premiums of Quebecers. The risk factor is, of course, a matter that is entirely up to the Caisse. It can take risks if it wants to, but we think that in an area that falls under exclusive federal jurisdiction, that is, where interprovincial and international transport companies are concerned, it should not take more than 10 per cent of that risk.

Madam Speaker, there you have it, the ultimate in Liberal authoritarianism and paternalism, just what creates a lot of problems, not just in Quebec but all over the country.
Since the Minister is constitutionally quite correct that the federal Government has authority to regulate in this field, why does the Government not rely on regulation? If the Province of Quebec does something contrary to the national interest in terms of its activity in the transportation field, or any other
Province does something that is contrary to the national interest, then take action. Why is the Government moving now to stop a provincial government from using its funds to create a public enterprise? Why is it prejudging the use of these funds?

Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Madam Speaker, in my opinion we are certainly not prejudging or drawing conclusions in advance. The bill is not aimed at preventing any normal activity by companies that are controlled by provincial governments. We have clearly established the rules of the game in an area that falls under federal jurisdiction, precisely because we want to avoid coming back later with legislation that would take effect retroactively. 1 see the bill as a preventive measure being taken by the government that is entirely appropriate in the present circumstances. As for reactions to the bill and recent statements by the President of the Caisse, who said that he had $1 billion to invest over the next four years in transport companies-well, let him invest them. One Member in the House has suggested that the Caisse purchase Quebecair. He can go right ahead. He has our permission. He can go and invest in any Canadian company he likes, but we say that he may not invest in more than 10 per cent of capital shares in companies involved in interprovincial and international transport.

Madam Speaker, what hypocrisy. Just a few minutes ago the Minister's colleague took pride in the fact that we have a publicly- and federally-owned Petro-Canada. This Minister is now saying that no Province can take similar public action. That is sheer and utter hypocrisy. It is all right for the CPR or Exxon to have more than 20 per cent, more than 10 per cent in the shares of transportation companies, but the Minister says it is not all right for the Province of Quebec. That is totally unacceptable in a democracy.
To get back to a mere matter of dollars and cents that the Minister perhaps understands, is he aware that the President of the Caisse has said that this regrettable authoritarian decision of the federal Government will possibly cost the people of the Province of Quebec some $100 million because the Caisse was planning to invest in excess of $1 billion in transportation over the next four years? Is the Minister further aware that, as a result of this reprehensible action of the federal Government, if it gets away with it, instead of investing in transportation in Canada, the Caisse may have to take its money and invest in Europe or the United States? Is that desirable?

subsubtopic: SUPERANNUATION FUND SURPLUS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. As a result of the June 1982 budget, it was announced that Bill C-133 would be implemented and that this would restrict increases in the Public Service pension plan by 6 per cent and 5 per cent for the next two years.
For the last year I have had a question on the Order Paper in an attempt to determine the amount of surplus in the Public Service superannuation fund. Would the Minister confirm that that surplus is in the neighbourhood of $14 billion? If that is true, can he explain why he is imposing the six and five program on people whose average pension is $8,000 per year, and on spouses drawing a Public Service pension whose income is only $3,000 per year?

subsubtopic: SUPERANNUATION FUND SURPLUS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 am not in a position to confirm the figure given by the Hon. Member, but I shall check exactly what the figures are. What 1 can confirm, however, is that indexing pensions of public servants is costing the Consolidated Revenue Fund-in other words, Canadian taxpayers-several hundreds of millions of dollars, and that the indexing subsidy is not taken from the contributions of public servants or the government's employer contribution but from the Government of Canada which collects taxes from all Canadians. So I would remind the Hon. Member that all Canadian taxpayers are contributing to indexing, and that what we are asking in this bill is that retired public servants share in the general effort being made throughout the country by all citizens to reduce inflation and stimulate the economy, and both pensioners and the rest of Canada will benefit.

subsubtopic: SUPERANNUATION FUND SURPLUS
speechtext: Of course, by separating the supplementary pension plan from the superannuation plan, the Government makes it look as if the indexing is costing taxpayers some money. That $14 billion surplus means that the Government is still ripping off retired Civil Servants.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (for the Secretary of State) moved
subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
that Bill C-95, An Act to provide for Government operated pool systems on combinations of athletic contests and events and to amend the Criminal Code and the Income Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Madam Speaker, in rising to participate in the debate on Bill C-95, 1 want to urge all Hon. Members of the House to support it. The legislation has been in the House having received first reading nearly a year ago. 1 believe it is very important in relation to a number of worth-while causes.
May I say that the first idea of such legislation came to me at some period after a group of very bright and ambitious young men from Calgary visited my office shortly after I had assumed the office of Minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport in the spring of 1980. Their idea was for Canada to host the Winter Olympics in the west with Calgary being the site, in the same way that the east was the host of the Summer Olympics, the site being Montreal back in 1976, which was a very successful occurrence. At that time these young men outlined to me what would be necessary in relation to financing from the federal Government, from the provincial Government and from the municipality in hosting the 1988 Winter Olympics if Calgary were to be successful in its bid to have the Winter Olympics awarded to Canada.
In the course of my discussion I made it quite plain that in these times it was not possible to contemplate the amount of money necessary for this worth-while purpose being provided from tax dollars. With the levels of taxation as they have to be in a country of this type in order to provide the many public services that are demanded and with so many demands on those moneys, it was not a practical undertaking for the Government of Canada to pay, out of moneys derived from taxes, the amount of support that would be necessary if these games were to take place.
I indicated, however, that it seemed to me it was the responsibility of a national government to co-operate in a worth-while project of this type. Not only had the Summer Olympics been tremendously successful in the development of our amateur sport relating to summer sports, but this occasion would give an opportunity for the advancement of our athletes who participate in winter sports in the same way. Not only would the Winter Olympics be beneficial from the point of view of the vast improvement in facilities which would be available after the games to the general public, but also the holding of the Winter Olympics in the west would have a permanently beneficial effect on winter tourism in this country.
It is a sad comment that Canada has lagged far behind the United States in relation to being able to attract winter tourists for skiing and for other winter sports, despite the absolute excellence of our facilities and the obvious nature of
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
our climate. This provides a great opportunity for attention to be centred in 1988 on the western Canadian Rocky Mountains and upon the advantages of that area for winter tourism.
I said that I felt that it would be possible for the Government to examine non-tax sources of revenue. I had earlier felt that it was unfortunate that the Government of Canada had given up the source of funds that had paid for a very large portion-retrospectively-of the cost of the Montreal Summer Olympics when the Government moved out of the lottery field, abandoned Loto Canada and gave it entirely to the Provinces.
However, when this Government came to office it undertook to examine that decision which had previously been made and reconsider whether the Government of Canada should go back into the lottery business. It was obvious that the Provinces were not very enthusiastic, to say the least, about the federal Government returning to the lottery field. Yet there remains a very real need for a source of funds that do not come from taxes that could be available to help the national Government meet its responsibilities in relation to sports, culture and, as this Bill provides, additional funding for the support of medical research.
If I may begin with the question of sports, 1 believe that it is quite clear that under the agreement which exists between the federal Government and the Provinces on the method of operation, the federal Government has the responsibility of supporting athletes at least at national and international levels of competence in the same way that the Provinces bear the responsibility of developing their excellent athletes on that level. In the same manner that Provinces have found it extremely important to have a source of revenue that is nontax in nature to meet some of those responsibilities which they have for their portion of such undertakings, there is a very real need at the national level for the Government of Canada to find such a source of revenue.
The costs of supporting artists in the cultural area and the costs of supporting our athletes and staging events as well as sending teams to international competitions have vastly increased. It is not reasonable to call upon tax dollars as the source of greatly increased financing for those causes, no matter how worth-while they may be.
Recognizing that the Provinces had occupied the lottery field, we searched very hard and conducted a considerable amount of research to determine how the federal Government might raise funds for these causes without, if you like, stepping squarely on the toes of the Provinces. We came up with the sports pool system that exists in most countries and which has been found to be attractive to the public, a good source of entertainment and a harmless form of entertainment. When I say "harmless form of entertainment", I use the words from the Royal Commission in Britain that investigated all aspects of gaming in that country. It gave a very laudatory approval to sports pools.

November 18, 1982
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
We considered the use of sports pools because they were popular in other countries and we had every reason to believe that they would be popular in this country, since it involves a voluntary contribution of about $1 by those people who choose to participate and research showed that they would have little, if any, impact upon support for the provincially-run lotteries. In the interest of maintaining good relations with the Provinces, we particularly wanted to find an area that would interfere to a minimum with the field they occupied, whatever we might have felt about the rightness of the Government also to participate in the lottery field.
That is the history behind which this Bill came into existence. I do not know whether Hon. Members are aware of the fact that our research also showed that low-income groups do not, as is sometimes the general impression, participate in these pools more than others. Before establishing the program we carefully considered the involvement of lower income groups. Our studies indicated that all income groups spend approximately one-third of 1 per cent of their annual income on lottery and raffle tickets. The most basic finding is, however, that the expenditure on games comes from the entertainment component of the family budget and does not compete with the essentials.
The sports pool is not a tax, as taxes are imposed or levied on the public. Consumer participation in the sports pool is strictly voluntary and allows for conscious funding by the population of those activities which they may not otherwise decide to support. It is a question of voluntary participation. The people of this country are proud of our artists and our athletes. We are all very pleased when Steve Podborski wins the world championship in downhill skiing or when Ken Reid does so well. We are all proud of Susan Nattrass, Jerry Sorensen and the junior hockey team which won the world championship last year, and we are proud of many other Canadian artists and athletes.

Mr. Speaker, during the next eighteen months Canadians will be attending a number of sports events, both national and international, and it is very important, and the Federal Government has a duty, to help Canadian athletes prepare for these events. When our athletes participate in sports events abroad, they do not do so as Ontarians, Quebecers or Newfoundlanders but as Canadians. It is therefore entirely legitimate and in the interest of our athletes that the Government of Canada should have an important role to play with respect to these events. Thousands of young Canadians will be training for and taking part in qualifying meets and many will later be competing in the events themselves.
The main events I am thinking of are the Student Games in Edmonton in 1983; the Canada Games in Quebec, in the Lac
Saint-Jean area, in February 1983; and finally, the Summer Olympics in Los Angeles in 1984. To prepare for these events, we shall have to set up training centres in co-operation with the provinces, organize courses for instructors, finance travel expenses and take on a host of other responsibilities as well. The Ministry of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) conducted a survey, some time ago, on fitness in Canada. This past summer we published the preliminary results of the survey which provide basic data on fitness levels and living habits of Canadians.
Using the survey data, Fitness Canada will establish priorities and formulate policy to ensure that the needs of Canadians in the very important area of physical fitness are met. It is clear that the revenue from the sports pool system, part of which will be allocated to Canada Fitness and Amateur Sport, will help us to achieve that objective.
I believe that these athletes do deserve our support and this is the way we can move in that direction. I emphasize again that the nature of the sports pool is very different from that of a lottery, and that appeals to a different group of people.
Let me make a very important point on the entertainment side. If one buys a raffle ticket or a lottery ticket, one buys a number, waits, and eventually finds out whether one has won or lost. The sports pools are different. First, one applies one's skills. If one is a person who follows the games closely, a person who knows sports and is a former great athlete like the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski)-

The other point is that, as a consequence of having participated in the choices of what the scores will be, one then follows the games more closely and watches for the outcome with interest. I must tell Your Honour my main reason for pressing for this legislation, and 1 say the "main" reason because 1 believe there are other important causes, such as the need for funding medical research and support of our amateur athletes and our culture. However, I must be honest and say that my greatest reason for pressing forward is that I believe that, in the same way the public of Canada supported the Summer Olympics in Montreal through Loto Canada it is equally important to recognize that the people of Canada would be prepared to give real support through the Government of Canada to the magnificent undertaking of a wonderful group of people who will stage the Winter Olympics in western Canada in the Calgary region. It is for that reason that I believe it is urgent to pass the legislation quickly.
With reference to the amount of commitment which is required, Calgary calculates that it will need $200 million in 1982-83 dollars in order to stage the Olympics. By 1988, that might amount to a great deal more because of the indexing factor. The Province of Alberta, under the enthusiastic leadership of Premier Lougheed, is fully behind this project and is participating fully. The City of Calgary is also keenly committed and is enthusiastically providing its portion of support. I am sure that Members of Parliament will not want the Government of Canada to do less for Calgary.
I also want to say that this Parliament will receive an annual statement from the Crown corporation which will be established. I am confident it will be successful and I therefore urge Hon. Members to support it.
Before I conclude my remarks, 1 want to extend my gratitude to several Hon. Members who have been very helpful in bringing the Bill to consideration. First, I mention the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) and the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant). I would also like to make special mention of the very keen interest shown by the Hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright) for this project in the manner in which he has kept in touch with me throughout the month that we have been trying to bring it forward.
I think it is a good cause. I know that some people have concern about the question of gambling, as they call it, even when the amount of money is so small, but 1 do believe that this is a worthy cause. We already have many lotteries in the country and this is a very harmless one of entertainment for a worth-while cause. I urge Hon. Members to support it.

subtopic: ATHLETIC CONTESTS AND EVENTS POOLS ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE GOVERNMENT OPERATED POOL SYSTEMS
speechtext:
This is the first opportunity 1 have had the responsibility of speaking on a Bill directly related to fitness and amateur sport. While I welcome the opportunity, I do not particularly appreciate the occasion. Quite frankly, I really wonder at the priorities given to the Bill by the Government. It reminds one of the old adage of Nero fiddling while Rome burns. To put it into more contemporary terms, it reminds us of the situation of the Government playing with the Hockey Select while the unemployment lines continue to grow.
At the same time, I can hardly understand the priority given to the Bill when it is already under the shade of legal process and in legal doubt. Ever since the announcement of the Bill was made over a year ago or when anticipated in September of last year, there has been a raging debate with respect to the legality of the Bill. Is it or is it not in breach of the 1979 federal-provincial agreement? We have now, Mr. Minister, as Members of this House know, a ruling of a court in the Province of Quebec which says that yes, it might be in breach of that provincial-federal agreement of 1979 and it might lead to some conflict in the court down the line. Nevertheless, the Minister throws caution to the wind. He does not wait until that matter has been resolved but comes forward with the Bill at this time.
I can appreciate that fact. I can appreciate why the Government might be fearful that the Bill might be adjudged illegal, and they want to bring it before us and have it in effect because they do not want to renege. I was somewhat surprised at the Minister presenting the Bill by outlining how a bright young group from Calgary came to him and talked to him about the need for support of the Calgary Olympics, and out of this the sports pool was born. We all know that the sports pool is simply an offshoot of the Government's election promise in February of 1980 and its burning desire to get back into the lottery field as it existed before. So he is carrying on a myth both with respect to fitness and amateur sport and as to how the sports pool came into being.
The Calgary Olympics have been dependent on Government money. What about the commitment given by this Government to the Calgary Olympics? The Minister talks in fine terms about supporting this great international event, but it is a commitment made by the Government only out of nonGovernment revenues. He continues that argument even now, that the support must come out of non-Government revenues. This just shows how much concern the Government really has for fitness and amateur sport and for Calgary.

November 18, 1982
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
I am going to dwell a little bit more on that as my comments are developed, but before doing so, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to refute utterly, completely and totally the propaganda campaign that has been waged with respect to the relationship between Loto Canada-and I heard it expounded again today-and funding for fitness and amateur sport. We are hearing exactly the same kind of nonsense now with respect to the sports pool as we heard earlier during the existence of Loto Canada and it is high time that these facts are made public and clear to all.
Loto Canada had a mercifully short, scandal-ridden term. We have to thank the Party on this side for bringing it to a conclusion and ending the existence of Loto Canada, which had at every turn brought nothing but disgrace to the Government.

speechtext: The then Minister responsible and now President of the Liberal Party spent many a Question Period explaining away one scandal after another, why they arose and why they should be dispelled. speechtext:
I invite the House to look at the Loto Canada income and expense sheets. There are still a goodly number of people on the Loto Canada payroll. It was simply happy days and open expense accounts! Several people have indicated that Loto Canada was a victim of growing pains and I agree. Loto Canada started its first year with an RCMP investigation into the awarding of security device contracts and finished its last full year of operation by squandering $14 million on a project that was contrary to Loto Canada's own regulations. This is the kind of growing pains that we do not like to see.
Scandals aside, Mr. Speaker, how successful was Loto Canada, and how did fitness and amateur sport benefit from that lottery? From start to finish Loto Canada generated a gross total of $725 million, and a net sum of $211 million. Fitness and amateur sport received $10.6 million or an average of $2.6 million a year. Great benefit to fitness and amateur sport out of that sum of money from the taxpayers and the gamblers of Canada!
More money was spent in one year advertising the benefits that were alleged to go to fitness and amateur sport in one year than they received in four years.

If fitness and amateur sport did not receive that money, where did it go? The question is
properly asked. Eighty-two point five per cent of it went to discharging the Montreal 1976 Olympics debt. The Liberal Government presented to this House, and all Opposition parties agreed, that we should somehow support the taxpayers of Quebec; we should not leave them with the debt of the 1976 Olympics. Loto Canada was then born to pay off that specific deficit of the 1976 Olympics, and it was to exist for a specific term of three years.
We already have extended one invitation, Mr. Speaker; let us look at another. Should anyone doubt the spirit, if not the word, of the Liberal Government commitment in 1976 to wrap up Canada's Loto by the end of the year 1979, let us just take a look at the June, 1976 minutes of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee. When our present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), then President of the Treasury Board, protested wildly at the suggestion that his Government would renege with respect to that termination date, in full rhetorical flight the Minister revealed his soul as one abhorring the very thought that lotteries, especially state-operated lotteries, would be continued. Time after time the Minister indicated that he would sleep a whole lot better at the end of this three-year nightmare. I have always enjoyed the Minister's speeches but that performance surely must rank among his highest.
We know from those minutes and from the revenue sheets of Loto Canada that both the Opposition, the other Members of this House and fitness and amateur sport were misled by the pronouncements of the Minister. Credit must surely go to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who saw through the theatrics of the presentation and warned that once involved in a lottery, the Liberals would never get out of it. Sure enough, in early 1979, the third year of that definite term, the Liberal Government introduced another Bill to provide an indefinite extension to Loto Canada's life.
The reaction of the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is not recorded. Considering the comments which he had made earlier, he must have winced at that obvious contradiction. The Minister's assurances given three years before were completely discarded as this breath of new life was given to a discredited Crown corporation, it is this proposed new Loto Bill of 1979 that has led to the myth-the Minister has left but he has left the myth that he has perpetuated-that millions of dollars have gone to the sports world.
Let us look at the facts of the situation. In its first short year of operation, Loto Canada netted $28.3 million. In its first full year of operation that net was increased to a total of $74.3 million. What happened after that? The next and third year of operation it fell from $74 million to $62 million. In its last year of operation the profits were $46.3 million.
These figures are important, not only because they are figures, but because they are the only real guideline we have as we consider the net that might be anticipated from the sports
November 18, 1982

pool. The proponents of the sports pool continue to announce in great exaggerated tones that $100,000 million will be received for the benefit of those who might be the beneficiaries. That we want to refer to as well. However, they have not substantiated how or on what figure it is based.
It is evident in the face of the stiff opposition from provincial lotteries that now exist that if Loto Canada could not make it how in the world can we expect the sports pool to draw the massive sums that are now anticipated by this Government?
Fortunately for fitness and amateur sports and arts and culture, Canadians put an end to that in 1979. One of the early acts of the Clark Government was to negotiate an agreement between the feds and the Provinces. They sold Loto Canada at a time when it had some value. It gave to the Provinces exclusive jurisdiction over lotteries in return for $24 million annually indexed to 1979 and a number of smaller considerations which would total approximately $20 million.
Not only did this agreement remove the irritant between the Province and the federal Government, which allowed the fitness and amateur sports and arts and culture communities to have a fixed sum of return and for the first time fixed sums of revenue on which to plan, build and organize programs, but it was not dependent on the number of Loto tickets sold.
The communities of arts and culture and fitness and amateur sport shared and are now sharing on a 50-50 basis the sum of approximately $30 million annually in addition to their estimates as shown in their budgets. We sold that lottery while it was still saleable. That was a good thing. If this Government had continued to hang on to Loto Canada and tried to compete with the Provinces as it was then doing, it would have been a sad state for all of us.
Let us turn to the sports pool. On the one hand, I do not subscribe to the view that the federal Government, in fact any Government, should be involved in lotteries. On the other hand, I want to say a word on behalf of fitness and amateur sport and in their interest indicate that they are being underfunded. Let us look at each of these in turn.
Canadians expect a good deal from their Government. We have the responsibility of looking after our national defence, job-creation programs, criminal law enforcement and civil law problems. I can tell you one thing. Canadians do not expect, nor do they want to see, their national Government cheapened by throwing its prestige and dignity behind projects and programs that are of dubious benefit to anyone. That is the problem we now face. The desire of the Government to get back into lotteries without a concrete figure as to what will be expended and might be realistically realized is a venture we are not prepared to support at this time.
Here we have a proposal that is based on the exploitation of the betting public. The Minister talks in terms of studies, but it should be pointed out that it is those with modest and low incomes who buy the largest number of tickets.
Has anyone recently been to a bingo game? There you see the gambling instinct at its best, or at its worst. Is that the kind of activity with which the Government of Canada wants to be
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
associated? If it is going to go that far, why stop there? Why not get into casinos or the numbers racket? Where should we stop? Where are we really going to go?
At one time the present Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Fleming) both expressed extreme concern with respect to the impact of lotteries on the poor. In fact, I was in this House on December 7, 1979 when the Hon. Member for York West rose and demanded an inquiry into the effect of lotteries in this country. How are those two Members going to vote on Bill C-95?
Setting aside the fact that the federal Government should not be associated with gaming, betting or gambling in any operation, we have to question the ability of the Government to undertake the project at all. The 1979 federal-provincial agreement on lotteries gave the Provinces exclusive jurisdiction in the field of lotteries. In order for the federal Government to operate a sports pool, it will have to demonstrate that a sports pool is not a lottery. One simply cannot accept the word of the Minister. It was nice to hear him distinguish between a lottery and a sports pool, but that is not a legal definition.
Thus far we have the opinion of one court. The Quebec Superior Court expressed the opinion that Quebec's Hockey Select, a sports pool, was not illegal because it fell within the confines of the 1979 federal-provincial lottery agreement. Hence the court in effect ruled that there is no difference between the sports pool now being proposed and the lotteries subject to that agreement.
Surely to goodness the Government would want to know what its legal base is before going further down the line and taking the action it proposes to take today. What will be the fate of the sports pool if it is eventually determined that it is illegal? I can tell you, Mr. Speaker. We will have spent millions of taxpayers' dollars on hardware, advertising and establishing this game and entering into competition with the Provinces. There will be long court cases in the Appeal Courts and eventually the Supreme Court will have to make a determination.
Taxpayers' money will determine what benefit will go to the beneficiaries of a vague and indeterminate Bill. Just to break even, the pool will have to generate enough revenue to offset the $30 million annually from the agreement as well as the start-up costs and production costs.
My point should really be clear. A sports pool is going to cost us money. 1 am not only talking about the overhead and mechanics; I am talking in terms of the immediate competition that will be entered into by Loto Canada or its namesake with the Provinces.
If it is limited to the number of persons who will be fans, as described by the Minister today, those who are skilled at picking the winner of a game, the numbers will not be great. It is bound to be a failure before it starts. Therefore, we have to concern ourselves with the alternatives proposed in the Bill.
Some studies have estimated the pool will not generate a net in excess of $20 million, which is $10 million less than we are

now getting. The Minister predicted an annual return of $100 million. I challenge him to state the facts and figures to substantiate that.
It is not generally recognized that it was the Diefenbaker Government that established an ongoing commitment to fitness and amateur sport so as to raise the health level of Canadians. That was to come first, the health level of Canadians across this country, and thereby to go on to win international medals and credits. But over the years the winning of medals has tended to overshadow the less glamorous areas of fitness, amateur sports, and recreation, as we know recreation. This has created imbalances in the budget allocation of federal dollars.
As a result of this imbalance, we have a situation where amateur sport is budgeting close to the line and those on the recreation side are faced with critical funding shortages. It is a credit to the ingenuity of the great national associations that they have been able to produce athletes to the degree and quality that we have now. It is to their credit that we are able to have our existing medal winners. With their record of achievements, accomplished even with these tight budgets, it would be much better if we had those advisers in fitness and amateur sports recommend and make comments on our budget deficiencies instead of the incompetent advisers we have had in finance through three mini-budgets within the last year.
Bill C-95 is supposed to be an effort to provide money for fitness and amateur sports. But I raise the question, is it? Who is to benefit most? The Minister was good enough to read out who the beneficiaries of the Sports Pool might be. The Cabinet's choice is remarkable. It is wide-ranging. The pool could benefit fitness and amateur sport, arts and culture, medical research, the Calgary Olympics, or any other worthy capital project related to sports and culture, or it could be a combination of these things. What is it going to be? Considering the Cabinet as it is today, no one is going to be able to depend or rely on any commitment in the future.
Going back to early 1979,1 read of a strong protest made by the then Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport and the then Secretary of State, the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), at a suggestion that Loto Canada provide money for medical research. They both said: "Oh, no, something as essential as medical research should not be included in a budget which has the ups and downs that a lottery would have". That gives you some indication, Mr. Speaker, of the attitude of those Ministers at that time with respect to fitness and amateur sports funding. It was not good enough for something like medical research, but it was good enough for fitness and amateur sport, and it should now be funded by the ups and downs of a lottery.
Arts and culture might have some advantage under all of this, but just picture the competition in a Cabinet meeting, with the different Cabinet Ministers, as to which one has the clout, which one has the force of numbers behind him, which one is going to get this kind of money. There is complete
vagueness and ambiguity as to who the beneficiaries of this sports Bill are. If we are intending to benefit fitness and amateur sport, why do we not set it out clearly, unequivocally, percentagewise or otherwise? Who really is to benefit from this sports pool?
We on this side of the House have no quarrel with the Calgary Olympics. We heard of the commitment and the representations which were made and how the sports pool was born. But as of this date all they have is a wishy-washy commitment in support of those games, and from non-Government resources. The money will come from Olympic stamps, Olympic coins, or any other kind of money that might come from the sports pool, if, as and when it comes into existence.
I can say that this Party is prepared to make a commitment to Calgary. In our view, the federal commitment should have been $200 million without any strings attached, an iron-clad guarantee. That is what we call a commitment. There should be a commitment that Calgary and its organizers can count on to the last dollar. But right now they still do not know what dollars they are going to get.
While we have no dispute with respect to Calgary, we do have some dispute with the worthy causes, worthy capital projects, which are referred to in the Bill. We have already seen the Government designate the Hilton Hotel as an industry in need of assistance. It well might be the Hilton Hotel that gets the benefit as a worthy project. They might put in a gymnasium to qualify. But what assurance will fitness and amateur sport have that they will get x number of dollars or a share of this commitment at all?
Before leaving the subject of beneficiaries, I want to point out again that even the term "fitness and amateur sport" is not defined in the Bill. We want to know whether the Government intends to give those moneys directly to national associations, to the Department to be divided among the beneficiaries in fitness and amateur sport, or will it thrive on the loopholes it has, as we saw with Loto Canada? We want some assurance that fitness and amateur sport as a whole will receive a fair deal on the division of the profits which will come from any sports pool that will be initiated.
Finally, on the other aspects of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, Clause 14(b) is completely unacceptable to the Members on this side of the House. This Clause opens the door to this Government's operation of any other lawful gaming operation. Can you not just picture the Cabinet determining what will be first in lawful gaming operations that should receive some share of the benefits, or what lawful gaming operation they will get into to bolster the fact that the sports pool is not going to bring in the money anticipated? They will be testing, trying to see which numbers or which game will gouge the public the most, and that is the game they will get into.
Bill C-95 leaves the question open as well to the Auditor General whether should he or should he not audit the corporation's accounts. Given the history of Loto Canada, we find it imperative that the Auditor General be charged with the responsibility of auditing this Crown corporation's books.

Mr. Speaker, I recognize that the Minister and that the two critics of the Parties had agreed to allow the Bill to pass some time this afternoon; at least, that is my understanding. Therefore, I will not take the amount of time available in order that others might have an opportunity to speak on the matter.
1 want to begin by saying quite clearly that we are opposed to the Bill for somewhat different reasons from those given by the spokesman for the Conservative Party. It is not an argument whether the moneys will in fact go to the places which the Government says it will, or whether or not there will be sufficient amounts derived from the sports lottery. The argument is whether or not this is an appropriate way to fund matters which are essential in terms of the well-being of the country.
I was looking back into the record, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you probably recall the circumstances surrounding a speech made by my hon. colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in 1976. On that occasion he said, as reported at page 13336 of Hansard:
It is because we believe that physical fitness, amateur sport and recreation are important aspects of Canadian life that we think they should be financed out of general taxation and, therefore, paid for on the basis of the ability to pay.
He continued:
We do not believe that aspects of life as important as physical fitness, amateur sport and recreation should be financed by gambling, which calls on the poor to pay for it, instead of taxation which is levied according to ability to pay.
We also feel therefore that this proposal to put the federal government into the lottery business for all time is economic retrogression of the worst kind.
Then he made a point that I think is borne out by the legislation that is before us today, when he said:
This makes it clear that the government does not take physical fitness, amateur sport and recreation seriously, and it makes it clear that if the government gets into trouble with something else-health costs, veterans' pensions, or what have you-which it cannot afford, it will say, "We can go in for gambling again,"-
That was a prophecy and that is exactly what happened. The Government has decided that it is unable to provide, from general revenues, the facilities for amateur sports, for physical fitness or for the pursuit of excellence in amateur athletics. More important, the Government has decided that medical research is to be undertaken from the funds generated by this so-called non-gambling that the Minister has spoken about. Those funds may be generated from the sale of lottery tickets, or the ability of people to choose who will win or lose on many
Athletic Contests and Events Pools Act
sporting events throughout the year. In that way they will engage in gambling.
A country cannot be run on the basis of games of chance. It may well be that as a pastime there could be provision for people to purchase a ticket and win a small prize, but essential services should not be funded on the basis of whether enough lottery tickets will be sold. Medical research should not be undertaken on the basis of getting a sufficient number of people on a given Saturday afternoon to bet on the outcome of hockey, baseball, basketball or football games.
If we are now moving toward that kind of financing of essential services, then the Government has ceased to recognize its responsibility and the time has come for it to give up the reins of Government. It is clear that if we believe the health and well-being of the people is important, then we must be prepared to make a financial commitment to that end. This goal should be pursued by encouraging people to take part in athletic events and fitness programs and to commit themselves to a higher standard of medical and physical well-being.
Over the years, many of us have argued that if we had put nearly as much money into preventive medicine as we have into other aspects of life, we would have cut down on the cost of making the nation more healthy. We would not have had to spend the hundreds of millions of dollars that we have spent on hospital care facilities. If we had spent money on preventing people from becoming ill rather than on making them well, we would have cut down on the amount of money necessary for medical care today.
This legislation offers nothing that will make the nation more healthy or encourage people to become involved in athletic endeavour. It does nothing to improve fitness in the sense of the general population becoming more aware and, therefore, more involved in physical fitness as a way of life. The intent of the legislation is quite clear; it will introduce an attitude in the country that gambling is an acceptable way for government to raise money. It is not acceptable, Mr. Speaker. I see my Conservative colleagues nodding in agreement; 1 am not exactly sure why.

That is certainly a point of information, Mr. Speaker, but as a point of order it fails rather substantially. However, I am always interested in anything the Hon. Member can add to the debate.
If we as a nation believe it is important to engage in international events from time to time or to host international events, or that it is of value to the country to be involved in the Olympic Games-and I believe we all think that it is-then we must be clear that there is a concurrent commitment to provide the necessary funds. But they must not be provided by some games of chance that may or may not succeed.
As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre said in 1976, the next thing will be that we will decide that pensions for veterans are too low so we will have to run a lottery. If it does not raise enough money, then the veterans will have to wait until the next lottery. The Government will say that that is a ridiculous suggestion. However, when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out in 1976 that the next
move of the Government would be the funding of health care out of lotteries, he was absolutely correct. This is what the Government is determined to do. When this measure passes- this game of chance or this gambling which we will approve in the House of Commons-it will then become a source of funding for medical research and therefore for health care.
I know that there are Members on both sides of the House who can see the destructiveness contained in such a measure and that there are Members on both sides of the House who would not for one moment want to see the Canadian health care system, either in whole or in part, dependent upon the whims of a few individuals or, for that matter, a significant number of individuals going out and betting on a Friday or Saturday afternoon on the outcome of sporting events. We are not running the Irish Sweepstakes here. We are not in the business of providing an essential service out of gambling. They may want to do it in some parts of the world; that is entirely up to them. But when we in Canada make a commitment to health care, health services and the provision of adequate facilities for health, whether it be in the sense of providing immediate care or research, we believe in doing it out of tax revenues. Also we believe that it should be funded in a way to allow the people charged with the responsibility of ensuring the continuation of the health care service to do some reasonable fiscal planning, to budget and to commit dollars for years down the road in order to complete the projects which they have undertaken.
This is what we in the New Democratic Party believe in. This is what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) has said over the years. This is what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre said in 1976. This is what we are saying again today, that there is no place in Canada for the running of a health care system funded in any way out of gambling; there is no place. I say to the Minister that if for no other reason, if the Bill contained no other flaws, that and that alone would cause us to rise to speak and vote against it.
Whoever advised the Minister to include that section in the Bill gave him bad advice. This is no time to play around with the health care system. This is no time to place in jeopardy research projects which are currently ongoing in every major medical health care centre across the country. This is no time to run risk with long-term researchers as they seek cures and solutions to many problems confronting Canadians. That is what this type of legislation begins to do.
It does not add to the funding. It substitutes dollars. Although the Minister and his colleagues may shake their heads, as sure as I stand on my feet the commitment of the Government to health care research in the next five years will be diminished proportionate to the amount of money raised by this fund. That is wrong.
The Government is already in severe financial difficulty. The Government is already having difficulty raising the

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
Beauchesne's Fifth Edition states that in 1973 the Government tabled in the House of Commons its views on the general principles governing notices of motions for production of papers. The following item states that the purpose is "to enable Members of Parliament to secure factual information about the operations of Government to carry out their parliamentary duties and to make public as much factual information as possible".
I now realize that these motions for production of papers have become a farce. On more than one occasion the Government has agreed to produce for me, but on one occasion 1 had in my possession papers produced by the Government which I found to be totally inadequate and incomplete. 1 complained to the Speaker and was informed that .that was too bad, but that there were no powers in the House to enforce the production of the documents. As recently as this week, an Hon. Member of the Official Opposition also received a ruling from Madam Speaker that, once again, it was too bad whether he did or did not get the papers which were to be produced by the Government according to the motion and there was nothing further that could be done.
Thus, as a Member of the Committee studying the Standing Orders of the House, I have suggested that we abolish this process in its entirety, that we recognize that it is entirely up to the Government to make up its mind whether it will or will not produce documents, the extent to which it will produce documents, that we request these documents via a question on the Order Paper, and then keep our fingers crossed that maybe we will be lucky. I am not at all enchanted with this procedure because we have just passed a freedom of information Bill and 1 feel it is too bad that we cannot get documents which are essential in order to do our work as competently as possible.
1 would like to refer to the essential subject, which is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the suggestion that there may be some bias in its reporting. In a moment I will illustrate. I have spoken on this subject many times over the years. In looking at some of the questions I have placed on the Order Paper, I did notice that to questions I asked concerning radio and the average percentage of listeners in peak listening times on those CBC radio stations in Montreal and Toronto, the answer was that at peak listening time in Toronto, Station CBL has approximately 7 per cent of the total listening audience. I am quoting only from Canadian Broadcasting Corporation figures provided to me. In Montreal the corresponding figure for Station CBM is approximately 2 per cent, and for Station CBF approximately 8 per cent.
Just to complete the radio picture, in another question I was advised that across the country the CBC English and French owned and operated stations, together with CBC affiliated

November 18, 1982
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
radio stations, had a total audience of 8.9 per cent. 1 have never suggested that that is not an important segment of the population of this country. Nevertheless, let us keep things in perspective.
As far as television is concerned, also in answer to a question on the Order Paper, again using Canadian Broadcasting Corporation figures, we find that, as far as English television programming is concerned, the CBC-owned and operated stations, together with the private stations that are affiliated with the CBC, are unable to attract the same viewing audience as the private networks. Furthermore the number of viewers tuned in to stations south of the border is almost as great as those watching CBC.
In the case of the French language stations, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Radio-Canada, does attract a somewhat larger viewing audience than the private network, and 1 think this is to be expected. Unfortunately, those watching the stations south of the border are not divided into English and French speaking viewers, although I assume they are all watching English television.
It amuses me when I watch American programming south of the border to see the number of advertisers from the Montreal area that spend their money advertising on American programs, despite the fact that they lose the benefit of the deductibility. Apparently, they find it more profitable to advertise south of the border, realizing that many Canadians are tuned in to those American stations.
I have discussed with the spokesmen for the Opposition parties that we should give as much opportunity as possible to Members to participate in this debate this afternoon, but since 1 made reference to the Applebaum-Hebert report 1 would like to put a few quotes on the record.
One of the important points that the report brings out is that the contribution of CBC television to Canadian cultural expression has been meagre. That is the word they used. The CBC has not been responsible to Canadian artists and has failed to promote them. The report suggests that CBC TV should produce only news shows with its own staff, and all other programming should be purchased from private producers. It is the hope of the Committee that by commissioning programs from independent producers rather than maintaining the present scale of in-house production, the CBC would tap a source of fresh program ideas.
The Applebaum-Flebert Cultural Policy Review Committee was exasperated with the CBC's bureaucratic arrogance and lack of verve. Its solution is to limit the CBC's own production to national news and current affairs, and have the Corporation buy other Canadian programs from private producers. It says that, unlike CBC Radio, television lacks creative initiative and intellectual leadership, and that in fighting to retain a position of power within the Canadian broadcasting system the CBC has developed a tradition of secretiveness which extends to virtually every arm of its activities.
It is on that note of secretiveness that 1 want to go back to an action of mine in May of 1973 when the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts were talking about the difficulty that we were experiencing as
Members of Parliament in obtaining information. As a result, and I suppose one might term it a fit of anger, I proposed a motion that the estimates for the Secretary of State for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1974 as they related to vote 50, payment to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, be reduced by $1,000 from $232,797,000 to $232,796,000. Mr. Speaker, when the question was put on the motion, it was agreed to on the following division: Yeas, 6; Nays, 5; and that motion stood.
We have never opposed the principle of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the need to provide services in remote parts of this country and the need to provide alternative programming and to promote Canadian culture. I have just read into the record that in 1973 the CBC's budget was $233 million in round figures. Today the figure is over three-quarters of a billion dollars. I feel that the public has the right to ask questions of its Members of Parliament about the manner in which these moneys are spent, and I deplore the secrecy in both Crown corporations, particularly the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that seems not to want to provide the public with the information it desires.
I wrote to the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on October 22. I was angry. The previous evening I had watched a program immediately following the Prime Minister's third speech in which they put on a satire on the news broadcast, "The Journal". I said: "If this is supposed to be an example of Canadian culture, then some of us would be less proud to be Canadians". The CBC, therefore, defines its role, and I think this is important on the question of bias, as follows:
The role of the CBC, then, in its current and public affairs programming, is to inform Canadians about the issues they confront as they decide upon their future through the democratic process. The exercise of this responsibility calls for identifying and exploring the issues confronting Canadians fairly and thoroughly, comprehensively and accurately, and for reflecting differing views about these issues, fully and fairly, and in a balanced manner, taking into account the weight of opinion which holds those views.

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
That is quite a mouthful. Also it was to serve the special needs of geographic regions, to contribute to the flow and exchange of cultural and regional information and entertainment, as well as contribute to the development of national unity. It might be arguable whether it actually succeeds at that, but that is in its mandate. That is a pretty big mandate for any corporation.
No one can question the fact that sometimes it falls short of achieving some of its mandate, but I do not think anyone in this room or any other room can deny that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been a major tool in achieving many of these rather lofty goals. The CBC is the main cultural institution in Canada. It seems to me that it is the most pervasive and most powerful. While it would be nice if more people went to concerts, listened to chamber music, recitals and lectures, the fact is that most people spend most of their leisure time watching television or going to the movies.
Or watching the House of Commons?

No, they are not watching the House of Commons, unfortunately.
Why do we have the CBC in the first place? It began under the Bennett Conservative Government. There was a feeling abroad that we would be inundated by American programming, and if we were going to develop our own cultural identity we had to have, in those days, one or two radio networks across Canada. Is this not also true today? That is why I could not really accept much of what the report of the Applebaum cultural commission recommended relating to the CBC. We established public broadcasting then, because it was either a choice of support by the state or domination by the United States. The same thing is true today, probably in spades.
We must ask if we need the CBC today. Does our cultural integrity, our social and economic fabric, need safeguarding, enriching, strengthening? Will private sector industries work toward these goals on their own, without the CBC? I doubt if that can be done. We have had the CRTC, and its content regulations and other protection but they have not worked out very well. The private sector has not produced much Canadian programming either, and I do not blame it. Private television networks such as CTV and Global have been forced, through economics, to use drama programs imported from the United States. Incidentally, as the Applebert Report points out, imported at a higher cost than these programs are sold to England. The fact that three networks are bidding for the same programs puts the price up.
With the best will in the world and despite promises made when they received their licences, private broadcasters cannot spend the money that is required to produce attractive Canadian programs. We should say to them that $100 million has come out of the CBC budget-1 disagree with the report, they will not get $100 million because their reach will still be the same, but they will get a good portion of that $100 million-and ask, what have you done lately to employ Canadian actors and writers who are fleeing to the United States? We must be doing something right. We have produced them. But they are off to Florida, California and New York, and we do not see them again. Broadcasters are making $1 billion in revenue each year. TV, radio and the private sector make $1 billion in revenue in advertising, minus costs. I was almost sick when I had to ask, as a person from the region, to go to the CRTC, and while I had the privilege of seeing these financial statements, which the taxpayer did not, I had to sit there and talk about community channelling and what that person was not doing to hire Canadians to do the work, only to hear them reply that they could not afford it. I was not able to rebut because the figures were confidential.
That is not the case in the United States. Most of what is done in the United States I disagree with. But any broadcaster who has a licence in the United States has to make those figures public. We have protected monopolies. They are protected in the sense that they are given the privilege of a licence. If anyone else tries to use the frequency, or in the case of cable, the area involved, we lay criminal charges and send in the police. But for the privilege of a licence in the United States, figures have to be made public. In Canada we have to rely once a year on Statistics Canada. How can any individual broadcaster, say, from Saskatchewan or from the Hon. Member's area say, that a certain number of dollars are needed to
November 18, 1982

hire local people? That is virtually an impossible thing to do unless the public has access to those figures. Parliamentarians have access to those figures and act on them.
No one knocks the CBC in the sense that it is not producing quality. The question is, are we getting $792.6 million worth of quality per year from the CBC? Are we getting the biggest bang from the bucks we are putting into the CBC? After three years of administering the CBC and other groups in the CRTC, I say no. A lot of money is being squandered unnecessarily. I do not think the CBC has the same group with the same concept it initially had. I think the death of the CBC came when it cancelled the program "This Hour has Seven Days." I think that was the downturn of the CBC. That program was too good.
Who cancelled that program?
The Liberal Government cancelled it.
An Hon. Member asks who did it. I sat with one of the producers who eventually became a CRTC commissioner-
Which Government cancelled that program?

That is a discussion I would like to get into with the Hon. Member at some point, confidentially. But 1 think the cancellation of that program was the downturn of the CBC. It became less adventurous. The CBC refused to do new things. Each time Hon. Members go out to the airport, they should look at the huge building housing the CBC. That is the CBC today. The bucks are not being put in the production end. You have very "funny" people doing production at the far end-people who produce the culture in this country do not sit in the CBC building. This building houses the middle and high management personnel for CBC who may destroy the CBC. There are more people shuffling ideas around so that the money is just not getting to the place where we want it. Production is where the money should go. That is the bottom line.
You cannot force people to watch Canadian programming just because it is Canadian, as I told the Hon. Member. Canadian programming has to be good. We put money out for productions such as the program on Louis Riel. That program cost $24 million, but it was good and people watched it. The program was sellable. 1 do not think Canadians would begrudge programs on, say, Fraser, the Plains of Abraham, or MacKenzie, or any number of things in our history. We have such a rich historical culture. Canadian historical culture is much richer than American, yet my children know more about Howdy Doody, Wild Bill Hickock and Jesse James than they do about Cartier, Champlain or Fraser. If the CBC took this money and spent it wisely-
