speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2) be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us tonight is one of several measures brought before the House in the budget of June 28. As part of its over-all strategy to reduce inflation, the Government is asking as many groups as possible-taxpayers, public servants, mothers receiving family allowances and pensioners-to help set the course toward achieving this goal. We ask these Canadians to accept a cap on the indexation of their income taxes and benefits over the next two years. But we do so in the fervent hope that all others, acknowledging this sacrifice, will voluntarily agree to commit themselves to similar programs of restraint.
Asking some Canadians to accept now what we can only hope for on the part of others was, 1 must say, one of the most difficult actions that we as Government have had to take. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that point very clear in his recent talks. After all, we know that we cannot give any guarantees to pensioners that others will join them in the fight against inflation but, at the same time, we are optimistic and believe in the willingness of all Canadians to participate in this critical national challenge.
The purpose of Bill C-131 is twofold. First, it proposes to limit indexation of the basic Old Age Security pension, known as OAS, to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent the year after. The basic pension, as all Hon. Members are aware, is payable to all persons at age 65 who meet certain Canadian residence requirements.
The second purpose, which 1 stress because of its importance, is that the Bill proposes that the full value of the two pensions paid to low income pensioners be maintained during this period. Thus, pensioners with low incomes who are eligible to receive what is called the Guaranteed Income Supplement, or GIS, or spouses' allowance benefits, will not be affected adversely by the proposal to limit indexation of the basic pension. In other words, these benefits will be doubly increased, that is, they will be increased fully, in accordance with the changes in the Consumer Price Index, and increased by an additional amount to offset the loss associated with the limited indexation of the basic pension. In other words, more than half of the Canadian pensioners-this is the key point of

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
this Bill-will not be affected at all by this legislation, and all pensioners will receive more in 1983 or in 1984 than in this current year, 1982.
This second proposal testifies, if it is necessary to do so, to this Government's long held commitment to assist the most vulnerable members of Canadian society, especially in times of economic difficulty.

The Government has always done its utmost to adjust its Old Age Security program to the economic realities facing all Canadians. Especially in recent years, which have inflicted the hardship of high inflation, the program's structure, and in this it is unique among all our government programs, has helped the aged to cope with the rising cost of living, and it has done so every three months and not just once a year.
Today, all Canadians are struggling with a new economic reality. By implementing radical, and 1 do mean radical, measures to reduce inflation, we shall be able to surmount our problems. Canadians at all levels of society must adjust to this situation, difficult though it may be, in order to avoid increasing hardship in the future.

Responding to this reality is what Bill C-131 and similar measures before the House are all about. Effective for 1983, that is toward the end of January, 1983, we propose that indexing of the basic pension be limited to 1.5 per cent of the current old age pension every three months, to reach an exact increase of 6 per cent for the full year. In 1984, similarly every three months, the pension cheques will be increased by 1.25 per cent, to reach an annual total of 5 per cent for the complete year.
No doubt, Members opposite will argue that this proposal departs from the Government's policy to protect the elderly against inflation. But 1 reject such charges at the outset. We certainly are not proposing to eliminate indexing of the basic pension. We are saying that pensions should continue to be indexed and will be, but for a limited time this indexation will be at a somewhat lower rate than the actual rate of inflation. For example, pensioners now receive basic monthly benefits of close to $247, or $246.92 to be exact. With full indexation, such pensioners would see their benefits rise next January to $251.12. Instead, we are asking them to accept $250.62, which is a reduction of 50 cents each month in the period between January and March, 1983. Over this two-year period of a special national solidarity campaign, pensioners would receive about $29 less in 1983 and about $52 less in 1984 than they would have received if no limit were placed on indexation.
Naturally, we hope that by working together we can bring inflation down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in those years. A year ago last November inflation was running at 12.7 per cent. It went as high as 13 per cent in July. It is now down to 10 per cent, the lowest rate since May of 1980. If we manage to achieve our objective, Bill C-131 will have only a limited effect on pensioners, perhaps negative compared to the expectations in the short run but very beneficial for the future. Of the more
than 2.3 million persons who receive the basic Old Age Security, slightly less than one half receive that pension and do not need any supplement, any GIS. These pensioners, the elderly who have some other sources of income on which to rely, and I recognize that often it is modest but it is more than what the vast majority of seniors have, are the ones who will see smaller increases in their monthly pensions.
In describing the provisions of Bill C-131 I have tried to describe frankly its impact on pensioners and the impact we hope it will have on influencing the attitudes of all Canadians.
We are asking 1.1 million old age pensioners to help lead the way in the fight against inflation. 1 am very conscious of the sacrifice we are asking of them. Their pensions will continue to be indexed, but at a lower rate than might otherwise be necessary perhaps fully to keep pace with changes in the consumer price index. 1 have to stress that it is not without reluctance that we make this request. We do so with the knowledge that these pensioners who are relatively better off, will be able to adjust accordingly.

Similarly, Mr. Speaker, I am very aware of the feelings of uncertainty that exist among pensioners generally, about the future of the Old Age Security pension. Everyone knows about recent rumours to the effect that the universality of this pension was threatened. I think it is high time these rumours should be laid to rest.
The Government has no intention of telling Canadians who have worked and paid taxes all their lives that the pension they earned, as it were, through their contribution to Canadian society, a pension they have been counting on, has suddenly disappeared.
Mr. Speaker, the Old Age Security pension is universal, and as such it is the basis of the Canadian system of income security for the aged. If we analyze this system, we see that whatever a person's income, there is a social contract, as it were, that guarantees a basic pension for everyone. This universal old age pension which is paid to all Canadians who are sixty-five or over, provides a starting point, and represents approximately 15 per cent of the average wage, that is, of the ideal pension. Now, does the fact that we are going through difficult times mean that we are not going to get our Old Age Security pension? 1 hope 1 have just made it clear that we are, but does it mean that there is no other way to reform the system? Of course not. I think there is room for change both inside and outside the system. 1 shall outline these changes quickly, although I am aware that it will take time to implement them. First of all, there will have to be a reform of private pension plans, which means updating existing plans with respect to indexation, survivor's benefits and portability, as well as providing that majority of full-time and part-time workers who do not have access to a company pension plan with a proper pension fund. However, this evening I am not
November 18, 1982

going to dwell on a subject on which public debate is to begin very shortly. 1 would prefer to indicate the salient points of future internal changes 1 feel are both possible and desirable. On several occasions recently, 1 have tried to make Canadians aware of the new world-wide economic situation and its consequences. For instance, in our capacity as national health and welfare Ministers, my predecessors and I have always tried over the years to convince out Cabinet colleagues to regularly approve considerable increases which were paid out of the public treasury and were added to our regular program budget. In 1979, for example, 1 told Canadians there would be an extra $20 a month per household for the spouse's supplement and allowance. That was an additional $290 million added to the program practically overnight, not to mention cost of living indexation. In 1980, I received parliamentary approval-easily, I must say-to raise the spouse's supplement and allowance by $35 a month for couples or single people. That was another increase of $500 million added permanently to our programs.
The significant aspect in all this, it seems to me, is that the current or forthcoming economic situation makes it imperative that we take a second look at the options open to us. I have come to the conclusion that we must be very careful before considering the possibility of allocating new funds to meet our social objectives, because the amounts involved in my area are always quite considerable, and I am fully aware that tonight is the first time I put it in so many terms before the House. A higher supplement for single persons in need, the political reality of the current economic situation and, above all, fairness in most cases, all those factors prompt us to consider the possibility of re-allocations within our programs and of tax exemptions for the elderly. This is what 1 mean. People generally think that we have only two programs, namely the basic old age security pension and the supplement which is paid to approximately 55 per cent of our senior citizens.
But we do have at least two other programs besides those but we seldom hear about them: the $2,200 annual tax exemption for people over 65, and the $1,000 tax exemption for those who receive what we call a retirement income or an income from private pension plans. If we could use a diagram to illustrate this and 1 often regret that it cannot be done in our proceedings, the overall distribution of these four programs would show that middle and higher income groups profit more from the age exemption and the retirement income deduction. The richer one is, the bigger the benefit from these tax exemptions. For instance, the value of old age pension, age exemption and retirement income deduction is the same whether a retired couple gets $10,000 or $50,000 from additional revenues. This raises questions. Under our present system, it is doubtful whether our intended goal can be achieved through indis-crimating programs that afford the same benefits to lower and higher income groups. One thing is certain, lower income pensioners, in other words those who are eligible for the G.I.S.
Old Age Security Act {No. 2)
do not get any tax exemption at all because their income is not high enough to qualify. This is why we say that tax exemptions as such are socially regressive. Therefore, this will eventually have to be reviewed from a practical standpoint, bearing in mind that most pensioners live on a fixed income, the real value of which they can no longer negotiate. What are the possible changes? The question is two-fold: First how can current tax inequities be corrected and second what incentive can be given to Canadians who managed to put money aside during their working life to provide for their old age?
So let us review rapidly the overall value of these programs. Roughly, old age pension expenditures account for $7 billion, some $300 million of which are recouped by the Treasury as taxes. But the supplement is not taxable, if I am not mistaken, it totals $2.5 billion. The basic tax exemption, the $2,220 a year and the exemption applicable to pension income, $1,000 a year, mean an indirect government expenditure of a few hundred millions in tax losses. Any discussion involving change and reform, must consider the overall budget, which means, a total amount of some $9.5 billion, before introducing any changes that would meet our intended goals. For instance, if it is agreed that an increase of, say, $250 million in the supplement of single or widowed recipients, 75 per cent of whom are women, is really necessary, the question is where to find such an amount in times of economic difficulty. Tax revenues have dropped; the cutbacks in the various departments have been used for job creation, which is clearly a national priority, and high interest rates still make any increase in the deficit unthinkable. I emphasize this last point because, in spite of the position taken recently by the New Democratic Party, there are people in this House and throughout Canada who believe that we can simply increase the deficit by a few hundred million dollars to achieve our pressing objectives. However, beyond a certain point, the interests payable on the deficit become intolerable because, from the point of view of a minister of social affairs, it is a waste of money. We must be realistic and avoid seemingly easy answers which would only prolong the economic crisis and exert even more pressure on all future social budgets.
So, we would have to find about $250 million, for instance, to increase the supplement of the 725,000 single or widowed recipients, most of whom are women, as I mentioned earlier, and living under the poverty line, while keeping in mind that it is impossible to find this money elsewhere in any foreseeable future. It therefore seems to me that wisdom dictates that we should analyze, apart from the first objective which is clearly related to social justice, the tax incentives to encourage savings with a view to improving them in the case of senior citizens. Is it not fair to reward those who have saved all their lives by increasing if possible-and I am simply asking the question- the exemption on investment income or by taking any other fair and appropriate tax measure?

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Such matters could be the subject of any future discussion with a view to improving the financial programs for our senior citizens. Having said this, 1 hope that I have made it clear that we intend to maintain old age pensions at their present level, and 1 have also dealt with two other aspects of our programs for senior citizens.
In conclusion, our senior citizens who are on fixed incomes suffer more than others from the effects of uncontrolled inflation. It is my conviction, therefore, that we must work toward a future world of six and five and later of even less inflation.
There is not a lot of room in which to manoeuvre, and I believe that all Canadians should support the measures of the Government to bring this problem under control. What it means in the long run is that all seniors will be better off. The fight against inflation must be our top priority.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of care to what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) had to say about this Bill to amend the Old Age Security Act. 1 did so because I had to listen very carefully. I know the Minister is suffering from a bad bout of laryngitis. I can sympathize with her because 1 know that is about the worst affliction any politician can suffer. Having said that, I can also tell her that is the last word of sympathy she is going to get from me tonight.
I am shocked that the Minister of National Health and Welfare would bring in a Bill like this. I listened to what she -had to say. It was a rather subdued speech, I may say. All the time she was speaking, I wondered what kind of battle really went on in Cabinet over this Bill. I wondered what she had to say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) when this proposal came up. Did she have anything to say to the Minister of Finance that would have stopped this mean, wretched measure?
Seldom has a bill come before this House so ill-conceived, so ad hoc in its approach, so mean in its impact or so disturbing in its implications. It is a Bill which exposes this Government's distorted sense of priorities as well as its gross mismanagement of the economy. Indeed, the Bill should never have come before this House. If Members opposite had any backbone, they would join with us in seeing that this Bill never passes this House.
When the Minister of Finance brought in the six and five program as the centrepiece of the June budget, he applied it to our two major income security programs, old age security and the family allowance. He told us that, beginning in January, 1983, old age pensions and family allowances would no longer be indexed to the actual rate of inflation as measured by the consumer price index, but instead would be limited to an increase of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance told us that those senior citizens who receive the guaranteed income supplement or the spouse's allowance, either in full or in part, would be protected against the partial de-indexing. Not only would the guaranted income supplement and the spouse's allowance continue to be fully indexed to the actual rate of inflation, but they would be increased to compensate for any loss in the basic old age pension.
He went on to say, with regard to the other income security program, that mothers eligible for the income-tested child tax credit receive up to an extra $50 per child for the 1982 tax year. We learned that the child tax credit benefits and family income thresholds for receiving the child tax credit would continue to be fully indexed to inflation.
I review all of this because it is important to understand two things. First, it is important to understand how shabbily a large number of our senior citizens are being treated under this legislation. Second, it is important to understand how unfavourably their treatment compares to that of Canadians who receive benefits under other income security programs.
This legislation is directed against the 1.2 million senior citizens who do not qualify for either full or partial guaranteed income supplement. What does this legislation do to these 1.2 million people? Assuming that inflation stays at its current rate of 10 per cent, each one of those 1.2 million senior citizens will lose $290 in the next two years, just over $70 next year and a further $220 in 1984. They will lose $290. Who are these 1.2 million Canadians who are being asked to make this sacrifice? Some of them, it is true, are probably well off, but 1 would say to the Minister, a great many of those 1.2 million Canadians are not. Some of those people are single elderly people with incomes just over $8,900 a year. That is where the cutoff comes for those who receive the full guaranteed income supplement. Those receiving more than $8,900 a year, whose incomes are just in excess of that figure, are the ones this legislation hits hardest. People who receive an income of $8,900 a year, or a bit more, if they happen to live in one of our major urban centres like Quebec City, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Calgary or Vancouver, already live below the poverty line. Their total income, Mr. Speaker, is $25 a day. This legislation will cost these single elderly people $290 over the next two years. To put it another way, it will cost them 12 days' income at $25 a day. That is why this Bill is so mean and ill-conceived.
This Bill also zeros in on another group, the elderly married couples with incomes of just over $15,000. They suffer a loss in income over the next two years of $580. That is what they are going to lose. That comes to about two months' rent for people in that category, and they will have to find that two months' rent somewhere else. Almost 25,000 single elderly people have incomes between $9,000 and $10,000, and another 25,000 seniors living as married couples, have incomes between $15,000 and $16,000. That is 50,000 elderly, Mr. Speaker, who are going to be hardest hit by the Government's six and
November 18, 1982

five legislation. The Minister said tonight, these are the ones who are to lead the way in the fight against inflation, the elderly Canadians. Fifty thousand elderly Canadians will be the hardest hit, single people with incomes between $9,000 and $10,000 or married people with incomes between $15,000 and $16,000. Those incomes are hardly riches or largesse. In fact, Mr. Speaker, they are hardly enough to live on in Canada in this winter of 1982.
Twenty-five dollars a day is what these people are getting to pay the rent or the property taxes, to pay the upkeep of a home, perhaps even a car; or to pay for transport to and from supermarkets, the doctor, the pharmacy, the library; to pay for food, hydro, heating, oil, gas. That is where the $25 a day has to go, to pay for the telephone, perhaps the luxury of a daily newspaper or cable television. It is really not very much, $9,000 or $10,000 a year in Canada in the winter of 1982. There is no great margin for extravagance. Indeed, there is no margin at all. Yet the Government is effectively cutting the income of these elderly Canadians. It is penalizing them for having the virtue of living just beyond the threshold of the guaranteed income supplement. They cannot expect to have the loss which they will sustain in the basic old age pension made up in the guaranteed income supplement. Truly, it is these people who are being required to bear the burden of the six and five legislation.
There is such a pettiness, such a meanness in this Bill, a meanness beyond justification, indeed, beyond comprehension. How much, I would ask, can the Government hope to save from these 50,000 senior citizens who are the first level to be hit? How much is it going to save by applying this six and five measure against that first group? Is it going to save $15 million or $20 million? That is a trifling sum to a Government, to this Government particularly, the biggest spenders of all time. But $15 million or $20 million to these 50,000 senior citizens is no trifle, sir. Even if it is split amongst the 50,000, it still is very meaningful. The $12 a month that it represents to every one of these senior citizens can make a big difference, the difference of having or not having a telephone, keeping the thermostat a degree warmer, or of eating nutritious food, fresh fruit and vegetables, even the difference of having $12 a month for the little luxury of spirit and soul, a frivility above the bare bones of existence.
This miserly measure is doubly hard to understand because of the double standard the Government imposes. These 50,000 senior citizens whom 1 have identified as the first level will be denied the full indexing of their old age security, they will be denied that $12 or so per month. But at the same time, a senior public servant is allowed to enjoy an expensive sabbatical in Paris, subsidized by the taxpayers. That sabbatical, Mr. Speaker, of that public servant would, in dollar terms, be enough to pay for the indexing cutback of some 1,000 of these 50,000 senior citizens. That is what it would pay for.
Ebenezer Scrooge was a miser, but at least he was an honest one. He denied himself as much as he did his employees and his victims, but the same cannot be said for the front benchers opposite. They simply do not comprehend what it is like to live on $9,000 or $10,000 a year, one-tenth of their ministerial
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
salaries. If they did, they would never proceed with this Bill. Perhaps, if they were more in touch with the people in this income bracket, they might begin to appreciate the impact of this Bill.
I do not know whether the Minister has had much mail on this subject, but I can tell her 1 have received a lot. I would like to quote from one such letter because it refers to the Minister's statement earlier this year when she told the senior citizens who were to accept this six and five limitation that they would have to learn to live with it. And this lady said, referring to the Minister, that she may be able to live with it, "but I am very much afraid 1 may not. I am finding that living through my second Canadian depression is much more worrying than my first." The next page of the letter reads as follows:
I have an income of approximately $8000, alimony, OAP and CPP. I am not eligible for any extra Federal assistance because I sold an RRSP last year. I live in a one room apartment, in an older building which is now out of rent controls, thanks to yearly 'legal' raises. 1 have a 15 year old Ford I can no longer afford to drive. Two years ago, I put every extra cent I had into a small house, 50 miles out of the city, considering it a wise investment. It is rented because I cannot afford to live in it. 1 can't sell it at any price, because of the financial situation, and can't ask enough rent to cover the increased mortgage payments, let alone utility and fire insurance.
Every ongoing, basic living expense has gone up this year: food, medical premiums, automobile insurance, light and telephone bills, property tax- everything!
I haven't dared to see my automobile mechanic or my dentist. I can't buy clothes, eat in a restaurant, go to a theatre, or think of a holiday anywhere, ever. And this is my Golden Age in the wonderful country of my birth?
That, Sir, is indicative of the response of many elderly Canadians to this six and five measure and to the cutbacks that they will have to sustain.
I would like you to contrast that with the treatment that young families with children received in the June budget. Again, assuming 10 per cent inflation, families with children will get $54 less per child over the next two years as a result of the proposed Bill C-132; $17.76 less in 1983, and $36.60 less in 1984. However, in 1983 when they file their income tax returns, if their family income is $27,000 or less, they will receive $50 per child more in child tax credit benefits. So families with two children and incomes of less than $27,000 will actually come out ahead in 1983, and will lose about $50 over the whole two year period.
Let me underscore what this will mean, Mr. Speaker. It will mean that single pensioners with incomes of $9,000 will lose $290 in this two-year period, but families with two children and incomes of $27,000 will lose less than $50 over the life of the program. That is the inequity, Mr. Speaker.
I would ask the Minister where she considers the equity to be in the proposals she is putting forward. Does the Minister seriously argue that a single, elderly widow with a $9,000 per year income should be sacrificing six times as much as a family with a $27,000 income? Does she also argue that such people should have the base for their future pension entitlement permanently lowered by these two years of arbitrary

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
indexing at six and five? Why are they being asked to do this? The Government claims it is because of restraint and to free the money for job creation.
A study of the figures in the budget papers will show that they make a mockery of the claim. The budget papers reveal that the amount the Government will save from the changes to the old age pension, the family allowance and the child tax credit amount to $10 million. That is all that is saved out of the great six and five program for seniors.
