speechtext:
But at the same time, the Government has found money to pay out $300 million in $3,000 cash grants to first-time home buyers and to any buyer of a newly built home costing up to $100,000. That means that the Government is giving $3,000 to people who can afford a $10,000 downpayment and monthly mortgage payments requiring an annual income of $40,000.
Less than a month ago we learned that interest charges on the public debt would be $990 million less than was forecast last June. That is money the Government suddenly found; it was a windfall. Is any of that $990 million being diverted to job creation? Not a nickel, Mr. Speaker. We have not heard a word about anything of that nature. We have to take the $290 from the old age pensioners with incomes of $9,000 per year to make up for the job-creation program. That is what the Minister proposes. But the Government does not propose to touch the $990 million that it suddenly found.
When I consider the kind of priorities that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance have sought to bring in through these various measures, I ask myself how they can stand there and defend them. How can anybody on that side of the House defend them? But after listening to the Minister of National Health and Welfare tonight, 1 conclude that she has no difficulty in defending any measure like this. She does not even seem to know what she is proposing.
On November 4 on "Canada AM", referring to the universality question, the Minister said:
All social programs, that means in particular pensions and all benefits for children, will remain the way they are. People are in the middle of an economic crisis and they need stability.
Well, they sure do-especially with incomes of less than $10,000 a year.
So why would she make such a statement when she had Bills on the Order Paper-Bill C-131 and Bill C-132-making very significant changes in the old age security and family allowance programs? One can only hope that she meant no further changes, but if not, her capacity for self-deception is truly remarkable.
There are only two logical explanations for this Bill, Mr. Speaker. One is simple incompetence. The Government simply did not know what it was doing. The second is that the Government decided to move away from universality in stages.
First, they would de-index the universal income security payments, such as the basic old age pension and the family allowance. This was to be followed in October by incometesting family allowance itself. If that was successful, they would then look at income testing the old age pension. There is considerable evidence to support that interpretation.
Much has been written in the past few weeks to the effect that the Minister of Finance wanted to cease making the family allowance universal. When caucus opposition made that impossible, he did an end run around the caucus and went public with the idea. The changes he suggests would be a radical departure from what Canadians have come to expect and accept.
Much of the retirement planning in this country has presumed the existence of universal old age pension. The $26.91 mothers receive each month to help them raise their children is seen as recognition of the important social role those who care for our future generations perform. Moreover, up to 30 per cent of the benefits flowing to those with the above average incomes, flows back to the Government in taxes.
If the Government really wants to bring some order out of the confusion of our income security system, there are much better ways to proceed than with this Bill. There is much that can be done through the tax system and otherwise to see that the funds available for income security programs are targeted much more equitably according to need. For instance, the tax expenditures represented by the exemption for dependent children might be used instead to enrich the refundable child tax credit. The age exemption might be converted into an income tested refundable tax credit for the elderly. Methods could be devised to pay out such credits monthly, so that eligible recipients would have a steady cash flow. We should in fact examine with the Provinces-and I have asked the Minister about this before-the whole system of taxation and transfer payments. This could be done with a view to making graduated levels of payment based on income and this, in turn, would strengthen incentives for people to earn more, as opposed to the present system with its arbitrary cut-off lines which encourages dependency. These are some examples of how the Government might better approach this whole question.
What we should avoid at all costs is what Bill C-131 and Bill C-132 set out to do, that is, to approach this important and sensitive area of public policy with ad hoc solutions designed to deal with short-term problems. The result of such an approach is inequity. Indeed, it produces results which are at cross purposes with the goals stated. Worst of all, the present inequities and the anomalies in our income security and retirement income systems are compounded, and a comprehensive solution is made more difficult.
It is no accident or coincidence that the Government which has given birth to this mean-spirited Bill is the Government which has dragged its feet for a year in bringing in its Green Paper on pension reform. How often have I heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare say that she will be bringing
November 18, 1982

in that Green Paper on pension reform next week or next month? I have heard it dozens of times. That Green Paper must be grey with age by now, and we still have not seen it.
The population in Canada of 65 years and over has risen more than 600,000 in the last ten years alone. That age group is growing at an annual rate of 3 per cent. This means that without any increase in real benefits, the economy will have to grow 3 per cent each year just to provide the revenue necessary to support pensions for these people. We must comprehend fully what that means. It means that the larger the population which reaches age 65, with little or no Canada Pension Plan, private pension income or private savings, the greater the public burden will be, since these people will have to be supported by the guaranteed income supplement. If we do not move on pension reform, we will find ourselves encouraging a greater and greater public debt. Even for the most selfish motivations we must act with urgency to see that Canadians now moving toward retirement have the maximum opportunity to make provision for their retirement income.
This means broadening the number of people covered by the Canada Pension Plan and reforms to see that it is adequately funded. It means making private pension plans and personal savings instruments such as RRSPs more accessible to people who have to move from one job to another, or work part-time, or drop out of the labour force to raise children. It means making it possible for women who work in the home to build up pension entitlements in their own right. It means early vesting in private pension plans and a change in attitudes so that people are encouraged to begin planning for their retirement from the moment they enter the labour force. It means all this and more.
We do have enough time, barely enough, to begin making these adjustments. The population from infancy to age 17 years, on whose behalf family allowance and the child tax credit are paid, is declining. There are about 850,000 fewer people in that age group today than there were ten years ago, and that decline is accelerating. This means that family allowances and the child tax credit will be less of a burden on the public purse over the next few years than they have been in the past. Also it means that an increasing portion of our population is of working age, contributing to the economy. If we use this period wisely to assist people in providing for their retirement, and if the economy resumes moderate economic growth with moderate rates of inflation, we can adequately support those who will be retiring in the next two decades.
Every year we let slip by without action makes it more and more difficult to avoid real crisis when the elderly becomes the largest single age group in the population. If we fail to prepare for it, we will have no excuse because the warning has already been given in the age group statistics of the 1981 census.
With a challenge such as this, with exciting new ideas proliferating daily on ways to make our major income support programs more rational and more humane, the fact that we are debating here tonight, a Bill such as this, is to me a source of anger and frustration to the Minister and her colleagues it should be a source of shame.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Perhaps there is a single virtue to this mean-spirited and ill-conceived Bill, a Bill which attempts to bail out the Government from the consequences of its economic and fiscal mismanagement on the backs of the elderly, near poor. Nothing could demonstrate more clearly than this Bill the urgent need for a comprehensive reform of both our income security and retirement income systems. The bankruptcy of an ad hoc policy of muddling through is nakedly exposed in this Bill. My hope is that it may provide the impetus for policies that will make it possible for those systems to fulfil better their original purposes, that is, helping those in need and ensuring a life of dignity for the elderly. That possibility, that hope, is no argument in favour of voting for this Bill. Instead my Party will vote to defend the lot of hundreds of thousands of senior citizens, elderly citizens whose existence will be made much more difficult because the Government singles them out as their primary target in the effort to correct its own economic mismanagement. My Party will be voting against this Bill.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). As I listened to her, I thought back to the time about two or three weeks ago when my little guy was getting underfoot at home and to keep him busy and out of his mother's way, I said, "Hey, son, go into the den and look up in the dictionary to see if you can find for me a name that would properly describe something or someone who would be capable of swallowing himself." He did that. An hour later he came back and said, "I have found it. It is a Tory." he said. After listening to the previous speaker, I can fully understand what he said. That Party several weeks ago waxed eloquent in support of the Liberal's six and five program. In fact, in this very House the Tories voted in favour of a component of that program.
We know in this House that when the previous Conservative Government was elected they were going to do exactly the same thing the Liberals are trying to do in this Bill. We know, and the people of Canada know, that if the Tories were ever elected again they would be as bad as the Liberals. I do not have to say that. The previous Minister of Finance for the Tory Government, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), is reported in the Sunday Star for November 14 as saying this:
When you ask somebody how you would go about cutting spending and that somebody is not in the Government, you're not likely to get clear answers because nobody wants to enunciate unpopular action until they're in the Government.
I do not see that particular Party as being any different from the gang over there. In fact, that Party would probably dismantle more programs in their hurry to reduce deficits and save their corporate friends from unnecessary tax increases.
We in the New Democratic Party unequivocally state our opposition to this Bill. As far as we are concerned, we will not be happy until the Government withdraws that Bill.

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
This Bill is an offensive piece of legislation and it should not be allowed to pass through this House. If this Government is allowed to get away with punishing the elderly in Canada, it will be to the shame of every Member in this House, Liberal Members included. In fact, after all of the things the Minister has said over the years in expressing her concern for the elderly, the poor and the disadvantaged in this country, for her to come out an hour ago and openly support what this Government is doing is unacceptable. I say that if she has any selfrespect at all she would resign in protest against what the Government is doing to the elderly poor in this country.
We will have no part of this Bill at all in this corner of the House. What this Government wants to do is place a limit on the only protection that seniors have against the erosion of their purchasing power as a result of inflation. The Government wants that limit to be 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. In addition, the Minister has said that those who only qualify for the Old Age Security are being asked to take a reduction of $55 per person in 1983. Our research shows a much different figure from that. Our research shows that the loss in 1983 is much closer to $77 per person per year in the first year only. In 1984 we estimate a further loss of $218.93. That is nearly $300 over the next two years.
According to our calculations the Minister is either missing or ignoring a couple of important factors. One is the smaller base on which the percentage increase is calculated during each quarter in 1983 and the compounding effect this will have during 1984. The other thing that has to be remembered, contrary to what the Minister is trying to convince elderly Canadians about, is that her facts are not the facts.
This is not simply a two-year one-deal shot. If or when the Government restores full inflation protection in 1985, it will be on a base figure that is much less than that used today, nearly $300 per person per year over the two-year period less of a base, in fact. What we are talking about here is a permanent reduction in pension income for retired Canadians and for future retired Canadians. It just does not last for two years. Because it is compounding and because we are talking about percentage increases and because we are talking about a much smaller base at the end of the period, pensioners will never regain that money. That money will be lost to them. The base will be less and they will continue to lose money year after year after 1985.
Over the next two years some 1.2 million Canadians will feel the bite of this Bill. The Minister responsible for the Status of Women will know that half of that number happen to be women. In a press statement on June 29, 1982, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) attempted to place the best possible light on her decision. She tried, Mr. Speaker, but in my view, she did not quite make it. This is what the Minister stated in her press release:
In keeping with our Liberal traditions in the area of social policy, the budget of June 28,1982, fully protects the lowest-income Canadians and the working poor. However the budget takes as a given that Canadians who are not in need are entirely prepared to share in the serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis.
Then she said, and I still cannot believe that our Minister of National Health and Welfare would even say such a thing, the following:
The sacrifice of pensioners who are not in need of the supplement to help the country get out of the economic crisis by creating permanent jobs will come to $55 per person for the entire year 1983. This is a considerable amount.
If the Minister does not believe that today's seniors make a sacrifice every day of their lives, then I do not think there is any hope for that particular Minister. The seniors who talk to me every day and those who come into my constituency office every weekend tell me an entirely different story. There is not a single senior citizen who relies on OAS alone, never mind the OAS and the GIS, who is not having a tough time every day in meeting the basic costs of food, shelter, clothing and transportation, not one. Wherever has the Minister got this idea that no one is suffering out there. As I said the other day, I don't know what she has been smoking.
The Government wants to wax eloquent about its six and five program. I have a letter here from a constituent of mine, a Mr. Marc Zwelling. The letter is dated November 2, 1982. Mr. Zwelling writes:
Have you noticed what's happened to milk prices in our neighbourhood? I wonder if it's a national phenomenon.
At the IGA the 2-litre size of homogenized milk was $1.67 last month-now it's $1.88. At the Mina-Mart (owned by Dominions Stores, I believe) it was $1.75, now $1.87. At the Red and White it was $1.75 and now $1.90.
I believe milk prices went up earlier this year, too, but not so much. We're talking about 12 per cent hikes. Whatever happened to "6 and 5"?
1 would like to ask that question, too.
While this Government wants to control the incomes of the average Canadian, including the elderly poor, it is doing absolutely nothing about the real causes and effects of inflation, which is price gouging such as that. I would be much more impressed if the Government were to tell Canadians that it wants them to lower their expectations but that it will make sure that the producers, businesses and corporations of the country will do their fair share while the Government controls their profits and prices. Even under previous attempts to control wages and prices, nothing was done about prices at all. Incomes were effectively controlled while profits were not. We know this to be true.
In an attempt to understand the number of people who will be affected by this legislation, I suggest that the Minister should perhaps read what the National Council of Welfare said in their analysis of the Government's budget. To save the Hon. Minister some reading time, I could read what the Council said after the budget came down. The National Council on Welfare in June 1982 said:
At first glance these measures may seem equitable. The large number of low-income elderly persons who get the Guaranteed Income Supplement-close to 1.2 million, or half of the aged population-will receive the same total amount of Old Age Security and Guaranteed Income Supplement payments asThey would have without the budget. The better-off half of elderly Canadians who do not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement will give up $77 each in Old Age Security benefits in 1983 and an estimated total of $291 by the end of the restraint period. Persumably they can afford the sacrifice.
November 18, 1982

However a closer look shows that in fact many elderly men and women who live at or just above the poverty line will be hurt by the budget. In its present form the Guaranteed Income Supplement is directed to those with very low incomes and is not available to many poor and near-poor senior citizens. When the limits on indexation come into effect next January, a single person's eligibility for the Guaranteed Income Supplement will end once his income from earnings-related pension plans, savings and investments reaches $6,123. This means that a single pensioner with a total income (including Old Age Security) of as low as $9,200-more that $500 below the poverty line for larger cities-will pay the same $55 sacrifice in Old Age Security payments as someone living on a moderate or affluent income. Over 100,000 poor and near-poor elderly Canadians will see their incomes reduced by this feature of the budget.
That is 100,000 poor and nearly-poor Canadians who, through what this Government is proposing will be driven even deeper into poverty. The Government has estimated that it will save $105 million as a result of this cutback. I am using the word "save" as the Government's word because it is not what we call it. That $105 million is being lifted from the pockets of over one million pensioners, and it is $105 million that those Canadians cannot afford to lose. They are people who have worked hard for our country over the years and have made life much easier for future generations. They have rightfully earned the right to a secure and comfortable retirement. They have paid for it, and now the Government is proposing to deny them that right.
This Government is making no bones about what it is doing. It is saying to the elderly in Canada, "Through our incompetence our country is in an economic mess, and we are making you pay for it". After you discard all the fancy words and phrases, that is exactly what the Government is saying it will do. For once I wish the Government would deal honestly with the people of this country.
For about the last 30 months the Minister and a number of her colleagues have been travelling across the country promising great reforms to the pension system. Is this the kind of reform the Government is talking about? Is this the kind of pension reform the Government is really considering? In fact, during all this time the Minister has clearly said in every public statement that the Government saw the need to improve the pension system. There was not even a hint that it intended to dismantle the improvements made to the pension system over the years.
As recently as April of this year, just two months before the June budget, the Minister assured Canadians that the Government had no intention of changing the rules of the game. In fact, in a speech to the Conference on Industrial Relations on April 20, 1982, the Minister said this:
The Government believes that, with the exception of a major increase still to come in Guaranteed Income Supplement benefits for single persons, the public pension system has served Canadians well.
Just listen to this:
We have no intention of changing the 'rules of the game'. We want to maintain indexing of the Old Age Security Pension and the Supplement every three months, and to retain the universality of the basic OAS pension.
Two months later, the Government changed the rules dramatically when it introduced its June budget. Indexing of the OAS is now capped at about 50 per cent of the Government's own forecast rate of inflation over the next 18 months. By placing an even greater emphasis on the income tested
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
guaranteed income supplement, the very principle of the universality of the OAS is being threatened.
In the same speech to which I just referred, the Minister explained the Government's further concern about those seniors who receive the GIS and are still living below the poverty line. This is what she said in that same speech in which she said had no intention of changing the rules of the game:
Additional expenditures of $730 million per year will be needed to raise a single person above the poverty line; the federal Government is committed to do this as soon as possible. This reform is of great urgency and will be undertaken on a priority basis as soon as funds are available or can be released from some other area.
In contrast to this expression of concern, I find the statements which the Minister made earlier to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to be somewhat more than interesting. The Minister appeared before that committee on April 2 of this year and responded to a question about why the $730 million needed to increase the guaranteed income supplement could not be taken from the money the Government had saved in its November, 1981 budget. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Government estimated that it would save $915 million in 1982-83 and $1 billion in 1984 by reducing transfers under the Established Programs Funding Act. Here is what the Minister said on that occasion about her concern for those individuals who rely on the GIS to at least lift them out of the depth of poverty:
The way I looked at that, as the Minister responsible directly for social policies and, of course, social justice in Canada, is, what will benefit most the huge clientele of whom I am the voice in Cabinet and for which we have these billions of dollars? And I subscribed-I must say without too much difficulty-to the hypothesis on which the budget has been developed that if we continue to have to pay large sums of money in interest on federal borrowings and deficits, that will be more harmful to my clienteles and the big budgets I need to protect and continue to see indexed every year than any other approach.
Then she said-no wonder she left, she is ashamed:
-therefore gave my full support to the budget, a budget which is aimed at reducing, not in a harsh way but in a reasonable way, year after year, the deficit of the Government. That was the basic choice that we had to make.
No wonder the Minister has left the House. If I were a Minister I would not want to sit and listen to my own words coming back to haunt me either.
So the Minister on the one hand seems to recognize that our elderly poor are living in poverty and that this is an unacceptable condition. She also says that when the money becomes available both she and the Government will take action to end this state of affairs. So what does she do when the money does become available? She and the Government and the Cabinet decide that what they want to do is to throw the money in to stave off interest rates as a result of deficits that this Government has accumulated. In fact, what they are doing to people on OAS benefits now they decided to do last November to people who are in GIS benefits, who are drastically below the poverty line and who desperately need help.
The Minister said that she had no difficulty in doing so. After going over the Minister's statements on what this

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Government has said over the last 30 months since we had the much-touted National Pensions Conference, 1 really wonder whether they have actually any credibility left in this country. They have certainly lost it in this House, and with this Bill they have certainly lost it with every senior citizen in this country. They say their intention is clear about what they intend to do about the OAS in the future in terms of whether or not it is to remain a useful universal program. 1 do not trust them one little bit, and 1 am quite sure that the average Canadian, at least from the responses I have been getting recently, would agree with that sentiment.
The Minister also said that nothing has changed for those seniors who now receive both the OAS and the GIS, and I suppose in some respects she is absolutely right. Those individuals will continue to have incomes far below the poverty line. On the other hand, she is absolutely dead wrong because things have changed and they will change over the next two years because the population of seniors at the end of two years who will receive OAS and GIS will be much greater than now and every one of them is going to have $300 less per year of pension income as a result of what this Government is trying to do today.
Again, that is not exactly my idea of pension reform. I always thought that to reform something meant to improve matters for the better, not to make a bad condition worse. That is what this Government and what this Minister have managed to do. Rather than opting to remove the weaknesses in our pension system, they have done the opposite. In so doing they have broken faith with Canadians once again. They have spent the last 30 months raising hopes and expectations across the country that real pension reform was on the way at last. Today, with this Bill and the June budget, those hopes are destroyed, Mr. Speaker.
I am sure all Members in this House get letters from constituents and from senior citizens in groups from time to time. Many of those letters are from people who tell me of the inadequacies of the pensions they get and how it is often difficult to make ends meet. Others make no bones about the fact that discussions on pension reform have gone on long enough, and it is time they get some action. I know some other Members received a copy of an open letter on pension reform from the Council of Pension Reform for Singles some time ago. Those who did I know will be interested in a few of the things they had to say.
They start out by saying:
This discussion will be different, inasmuch as it is written by single pensioners who have banded together to form their own Council on Pension Reform for single women/men and is probably the first such paper ever written.
They say:
The majority of women, single, now in their eighties and up, many of whom were in the labour force through two wars and a depression, up to fifty years, who merely because they were born too soon also have no "personal protection under the Canada Pension Plan" ... Is it being taken for granted that they are all tucked away in public wards in nursing homes, senile and unable to care for themselves? We can assure anyone interested that there are not enough nursing homes in Canada to hold them, but no matter where they are living they still need to pay living costs which increase by the minute.
They go on to say:
We are the same segment of Canadians who did not qualify for Canada Pension, are the same Canadians who, when they retired at sixty-five years of age had to live for five years on their small wartime savings until they received their Old Age Security at seventy years of age. It must also be remembered that for women of that day private pension plans were practically unknown. These are also the same seniors who are ignored by pension reformists, seniors organizations and Government alike. All reformists have to suggest is an increase in Old Age Security on a means test.
It is an acknowledged fact that singles have been, and are today, $800 and up below the poverty line in Old Age Security. Couples are slightly above the poverty line. This has been true year after year and nothing has been done for singles. Singles who through wartime and depression sacrificed in order to make some preparation for retirement are now being penalized by means tests. There were no trips to Europe in their day and few luxuries, nor are there now. Their standard of living is slipping and they have no relief.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, they say this and they make more sense than anything I have heard in this place tonight. They say:
We believe it is time to combine Old Age Security and Guaranteed Income Supplement as one Old Age Security Pension without a means test. The present two plans are expensive to administer and are causing so much division, cheating and bitterness against the Government amongst pensioners who made some provision for their retirement and who are being penalized for having done so, that it would appear that everyone, including the Government would in the long run be better off both financially and in good-will, by combining the two pensions.
Most if not all the seniors that I know who are forced to apply for the GIS feel exactly the same way. They deeply resent the welfare stigma attached to the plan through the requirement that they have to prove their poverty before they can receive the GIS. Our personal pride in being able to hold our head up to friends and neighbours is valuable to all of us. It is even more so to elderly people, and it is unconscionable that this Government wants to make life for thousands of older individuals even more difficult than it already is.
The National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation has also noted to the Government that literally hundreds of thousands of seniors are receiving $85 a month less than that required to provide the absolute minimum of food, clothing and shelter.
A number of seniors have told me that they are confused by the complexity of pension programs or, indeed, what may be available to them from time to time. It is no wonder when you look at this mish-mash that serves as a pension system. In Canada we have private plans that cover only 50 per cent of the male work force and one-third of the female work force. Even at that, employer-sponsored plans only account for less than 10 per cent of the over-all income of present senior citizens. At the federal level we have the old age security pension, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the Canada-Quebec Pension Plan. In addition to that, because of the inadequacies of these programs, the richer Provinces have introduced their own supplementary programs. Ontario has its Guaranteed Annual Income System, GAINS. Alberta has the Alberta Assured Income Plan. Both of these are means tested.
It is no wonder that people are confused. The fact that all those bits and pieces are in place is a clear indication that
November 18, 1982

something is out of place here. Why should individuals have to rely on a whole number of programs in order to receive an income on retirement?
Surely an adequate pension is a right and not a privilege. Surely every Canadian should have available a decent and adequate pension, regardless of sex, marital status, income class and previous employment history. Surely it is reasonable to expect on retirement that individuals will have an income that is above the poverty line and that the income will grow with the standard of living.
Pensions must be viewed as inter-generational transfers. They must connect the living standards of pensioners to the general standard of living. There is no question that public pensions must be expanded immediately to guarantee a poverty-free and secure standard of living for Canada's two million seniors.
It is only the federal and the provincial Governments that are in a position to ensure that this is done. In the public debate over the past 30 months, a consensus has emerged, at least from the majority, that some basic improvements must be made quickly. In fact, the Minister has publicly said there is a need to increase pensions immediately by $25 a month. She said that less than three weeks ago, I believe.
Even the corporation of William M. Mercer, hardly a socialist organization, has said that pensions should be increased now because it is necessary by a minimum of $100 a month. It is obvious to Members of this Party that the Old Age Security must be increased and the Canada Pension Plan expanded.
In conclusion I will say that if this Bill is not withdrawn by the Government it is the view of this Party that it cannot be allowed to be rammed through the parliamentary process. If and when it is referred to committee, individuals and organizations wishing to have input into this measure must have an opportunity to do so. The consequences of this legislation on the incomes of the elderly in Canada makes it imperative that this be done. Finally, if this Government is serious, which is questionable, about redistributing income in this country by directing the available funds to those most in need, I can think of a better place to start rather than attacking Canada's elderly population, that is, to overhaul the tax structure in this country. That is where the unfairness lies, and it is high time the Government made it equitable to all Canadians.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to say a few words on Bill C-131 to amend the Old Age Security Act. Before doing so, 1 would like to point out that the last speaker for the New Democratic Party said that in supporting the six and five program we in this Party imply that we support as well the principles of Bill C-131 to reduce the old age pension. The Hon. Member knows very well that we supported the six and five program as it applied to civil servants. It had nothing to do with old age pensioners.
It is common knowledge in this House and across the country that the NDP can say anything irresponsibly, promise anything, knowing full well and sighing with relief at the same
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
time that they will never be in a position of national power to put their money where their mouth is or to take their feet out of their mouth. As a veterinarian, 1 am more than willing to offer my services for medical assistance, surgery or otherwise-

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: For foot and mouth disease.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes, for foot and mouth disease. Most of them in the NDP are in dire need of it. 1 am sure I can call on my hon. friend from Guelph, a colleague and classmate of mine, to give assistance if I require it. I do not think 1 need any assistance, Jim.
To get into the substance, if this Bill is passed into law, it would limit the incease in the basic old age pension to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. In other words, old age pensioners are being told that, like it or not, they will have to take a cut in their meagre pensions to conform with the six and five policy of restraint.
I believe that the six and five program is a small step in the right direction, but I believe that the Government in its deliberation on this matter, should have considered the exemption of old age security recipients from this legislation. Many senior citizens have a bad enough time as it is without having to cope with a decrease in their pension.
When one considers a 10 per cent inflation rate in the country coupled with a 6 per cent decrease in the pension, one must realize that this will have a devastating effect on the seniors of our country, many of whom are barely managing now to cover the cost of only the bare essentials of life such as food, clothing, higher and higher rents and escalating drug costs.
This is a terrible slap in the face to our seniors. When one reflects on the hardships and devastations they experienced and lived through, two world wars and a devastating depression of the 1930s, one must conclude that this is one heck of a way to express our gratitude and thanks, by cutting back on their pensions. This is a terrible injustice and should not be allowed to take place.
1 do not want to leave the impression that 1 am not in favour of restraint. I believe restraint in government spending is adamant, and when I say government I mean all three levels, federal, provincial and municipal. However, surely common sense should tell us, and common sense should prevail, that restraint should not be imposed on those citizens who can least afford it, our senior citizens. Equity and fariness must be exercised in this case. However, if Bill C-131 is passed, it will be throwing equity and fairness out the window.
Simply put, it is not fair riding out the recession on the backs of our senior citizens. Seeking restraint from those who can afford it, I can go along with, but seeking restraint from those who in no earthly way can afford it is unthinkable to say the least.
The effects of inflation on the elderly are devastating. Today, 20 per cent or some 600,000 of them live in poverty.

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
We know as well that senior citizens are forming an ever-increasing section of our population.
That is why I believe the time has come, and 1 think it is long overdue, to take a serious look at all our pension needs, public and private, to ensure that at the time of retirement, one should be able to live our's declining years without fear of deprivation and without the worry of having enough funds to live on.
1 know that over the years there has been a lot of discussion and a lot of studies regarding pensions. As worthwhile as they have been, I think the time has come to take the bull by the horns and come forth with action. I firmly believe that all Canadians are now more ready than ever to make the necessary contribution from their salaries and paycheques to ensure security in their old age. All I can say is, let's get on with it.
I believe all Members of this House would give speedy passage to any bill brought forth to make this a reality. It is important to understand that we must get away from the stereotype idea that pension funds are not part of an obligation on each and every one of us, that we only put money away if we can spare it. I believe that pensions should be looked at, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said, as a deferred income that we will draw upon once we leave the workplace. We must make sure as well that all pensions in force should not be drained of funds by being over-extended in the form of loans to the Provinces or otherwise. There should be sufficient funds, wisely invested, to ensure the presence of actual money there, not just a paper figure, but actual money to take care of any crisis or emergency. This is one area where bankruptcy would be a terrible disaster.
It is a sad state of affairs, Mr. Speaker, that in this so-called enlightened age, only 28 per cent of women in the labour force today are covered by some sort of a pension plan, and over half of that 28 per cent are in some level of Government. Another thing to remember is that our present pension system is not geared to the problems and situations faced by women. For example, what if a woman drops out of the labour force to have children? No allowance is made at all for this. Benefits are not adjusted for the period she is away because her pension is based on total earning and working life, which in this case is smaller and shorter. But her need for pension coverage is no less necessary after her most productive years are over .
A housewife who finds herself widowed is in a very similar position. Her career was as a housewife, for which she received no pension because most pensions collected by a husband are non-transferable. She cannot collect on that pension even though she contributed so many years as a housewife. She is left with what amounts to poverty line pension, unless otherwise provided for.
What can be done to rectify some of the problems I have mentioned? There have been a number of proposals offered to help women overcome these handicaps. One suggestion which
has been talked about for a while is to allow housewives to contribute to CPP. The question of whether contributions should be voluntary or not is central to whether the plan would work. Some housewives simply cannot afford to pay into the system, but their need is no less obvious. Another proposal is to allow more housewives to collect contributions from private pension plans of deceased spouses. Survivor's benefits, to my mind, are important if women are to maintain their independence. Another idea put forward to help women out in the case of a marriage breakdown, was to make it mandatory that pension credits in a private pension plan held by the husband be split 50-50 on divorce.
Another proposal is to have fully portable indexed pensions. Few pension plans today are portable, except for Government employees. When you change jobs, you cannot take credits with you, so you loose your contributions. These are some of the solutions offered. It goes without saying they do not solve all the problems, but they are a start. Right now, we are anxiously awaiting the Government's so-called Green Paper on pension reform. We have been told it will be out soon. Hopefully, the report will lead to some meaningful and substantial reforms which are so rightly deserved by the majority of the Canadian population.
Another related matter concerning senior citizens and pensions, Mr. Speaker, is the subject of old age. You may ask the question, how old is old? That is a question which has puzzled physicians, economists, business leaders, labour, government officials and every man and woman in our country. Two thousand years ago, the average life expectancy was only 22 years. Seventy-five years ago, in Canada, the life expectancy for the male was 48 years and for the female, 51 years. However, the average life expectancy today for a male is somewhere around 74 years, and for a female between 76 and 78 years. Today's 65-year old man or woman probably has greater vigour, greater stamina and better health than the 50-year old man or woman in the 1900s. There is no question that the lifespan of man will continue to increase. Perhaps within the lifespan of many Canadians alive today, one-tenth of our population will live to be 100 or older. Soon, perhaps within a generation, active, vigorous men and women of 85 years or more will make up a substantial group in every community.
However, because of the longer lifespan of people today, there is another area of importance which will have to be looked into, that is, the impact this will have on our national economy. I think the time has come when we must review the retirement practices in industry. In the very near future we may find it desirable to go in the direction of voluntary retirement, depending upon the health of each worker. It may even be desirable to defer retirement in many cases from age 65 to 70 or 75. Regardless of what may happen, however, the human values of forced retirement at age 65 cannot be overlooked. What happens to the person at age 65 who is told that his usefulness in the labour force is over? He is no longer allowed to contribute. He is suddenly cut off from his working companions of many years. Just because he turned 65 years of age he
November 18, 1982

is supposed to stop functioning. How can you equate this kind of treatment when today these very same people have the most active seniors' and senior citizens' organizations in the history of our country. In view of this, how can labour say with any conviction that seniors are no longer able to contribute to the labour force? 1 do not think there is anything magical or sacred about the age of 65. Retirement at age 65 has been arbitrarily adopted and blindly accepted. Chronological age is not a barometer which necessarily indicates the physical age of a person. A person forced to retire due to the age formula loses more than just an income. In many cases, and I have seen some, as 1 imagine other Members of the House have, a person is faced with emotional problems every bit as serious as economic ones.
In our society, work has come to mean recognition as well as a feeling of being a useful member of the community. Some retirees, through an inward feeling of uselessness and insecurity, become melancholy and unhappy, and at times quite ill, which can only be overcome by work. During World War II, many elderly people went back to work in Canada. I think there were some 250,000 of them. Their employers learned to respect their steady and reliable performance. Recently in the U.S., the National Association of Manufacturers polled a group of business leaders on their attitudes toward elderly workers. Significantly, the president of one of the companies stated: "We choose and select when we hire people and I see no reason why we cannot do the same when we retire them." There are those and there will be those tomorrow who will want to retire. There are those today and there will be those tomorrow who will need to retire because of ill health or inability to do their job. Retirement is not a bad thing, but forced retirement of a man or a woman who is healthy, who wants to work, is bad both for the man and the woman and for our country as a whole.
Older citizens of Canada have a treasury of skills and experience that could be used in so many ways in every community. Seniors want to be constructive and productive. Our society has to find ways to keep them working if they so wish. To accomplish this, we must stop using one myth after another to justify age discrimination in employment. We must stop believing the myth that a young labour force guarantees greater production and less overhead. That may be true in the case of a man operating a jackhammer, but there are all kinds of occupations where the elderly are just as productive as their juniors.
We must also stop believing the myth of the heavy cost burden involved in hiring the elderly. Department of Labour statistics show that putting an older person on the payroll, including all the fringe benefits, costs only a few pennies an hour more than it would to hire a younger person. We must stop believing the myth that older persons are absent from their jobs more than younger persons. The very opposite is true. The notion that older persons are ready to be put on the shelf, is about the silliest form of prejudice which still exists. It is simply incredible that we have permitted our society to become so youth oriented that the job market starts to close after a person reaches 40.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
What is needed in Canada, today, Mr. Speaker, is a drastic change of attitude. We have to get away from the notion that elderly people have done their part and should be put on the shelf. Our attitudes must change so that retirement from active, productive living should be by choice and not by compulsion because of age. Many seniors have no desire to stop work. Many seniors are able to work and want to work, but modern methods of business and industry deny them the opportunity to do so. The performance of Government in recent years for the betterment of senior citizens permits a small amount of pride. The challenges of today must give us even greater energy, greater dedication and a greater commitment to get on with the job, not only of creating a better Canada, but a better deal for all senior citizens. If we succeed in changing the popular conception of age and return those seniors who wish once more to the role of national productivity, I think we will then meet our two greatest needs. These are the need for a chance to make a living, and the great emotional satisfaction that comes from being useful, from being respected for one's productivity rather than being respected just for being elderly.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the saying that we should never judge anyone until we have walked a mile in his moccasins is an excellent dictum. Tonight, I wonder if any of us is prepared to walk in the moccasins of those who are entirely dependent on a pension.
I remember when there was a pension of $20 per month for those aged 70 and over. In those days, though, you could buy five pounds of hamburger for 15 cents, so $20 went a long way. Through the years the pension has increased in accordance with the requirements of providing food, clothing and shelter for the human body. Eventually, the pension reached a reasonable amount; then inflation came along. That made quite a difference.
The Government made wonderful speeches to the effect that the pensioner could not live on that amount when the cost of living was so high, and so the pension would be indexed. The whole purpose of indexing was that food, shelter and clothing for the human body could still be supplied.
How many times have I heard Ministers and backbenchers opposite, and even Members on this side of the House, remark on what an excellent thing indexing is. The former minister of finance was asked how pensioners were going to continue to live on their pensions when the cost of energy and almost everything else was going up. He answered that the pension was being indexed so that they could live on it. The amount indexing brought in never equalled the amount of increase in the price of energy, however, but it helped. The whole purpose of indexing, as put forward by the Government and, I suppose, by Members on this side of the House, was to enable people to continue to enjoy a reasonable standard of living.
I remember being on a platform in the beautiful City of Drumheller, which is nestled in the canyon of the Red Deer River, when 200 or 300 people had turned out for an auction

November 18, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
at a church. One question that was put to each candidate was about the stand they would take on indexing. One candidate said, "1 am against indexing; it costs too much money and we cannot afford it". Another candidate said, "I am not in favour of indexing, even though I am getting an indexed pension myself." When it came my turn I simply asked the people, "If you do not have indexing, how are the aged going to live?" That is the only purpose for it, Mr. Speaker. It is not a gift, a gratuity or a Christmas present; it is essential if a person is to be able to pay for food, clothing and shelter.
I have been in the homes of senior citizens and pensioners who receive the full basic pension and the guaranteed income supplement and their assured income from the Province. Some are still having a rough time making ends meet. I am sure you realize, Mr. Speaker, that energy costs have gone up by 15 to 30 per cent. I went into the home of a pensioner in Edmonton last winter. He was wearing a big, woolly sweater and his wife was wearing a night robe of some kind. It was only eight o'clock at night. I asked him why he was wearing his sweater, but I soon found out why. The house was cold. He said that the Government had asked the people to co-operate, to keep costs down and not to use too much energy. He said that he wanted to co-operate with the Government, so there he was, shivering.
I shivered too and I kept my overcoat on. It is still chilly in that home, Mr. Speaker, but they wear woollies in order to cooperate.
If this Bill passes, the aged will co-operate, but there will be some cold ones amongst them and there will be some hungry ones. They will have diseases and they will die sooner because they will not be able to afford the things that they should have.
Do we want history to record that we did not look after our senior citizens properly-those who have served this country? People who are now aged 65 were born in 1917. They went through a few good years after the first World War, and then came the depression. People who have not lived through the depression will never know what it was like, but people who did live through it, those who are 65 years of age today, still suffer because of the malnutrition, lack of food and heat that they experienced. If they had to cut their own food or haul their own coal in order to keep warm, that is what they did. And all through the years of World War II they co-operated.
I knew a miner who was 83 years of age when World War II started. After the first World War miners were lucky if they got three months of work a year. But we needed coal for the war effort, and so he got his carbide lamp and his old mining clothes and went back into the mine to help his country, in World War II. It took a few years off his life, but he cooperated.
Senior citizens have already paid the price and we should not ask them to pay more. They should have the right to live well now.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

Mr. Speaker, tonight we will discuss one example of utter waste of the taxpayer's money which the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) blatantly defended as being in the national interest, saying, "The cost of distribution is completely justified in the national interest." Five hundred and seventy-six packages containing three maps, a photo of the Minister of State for Mines with the Governor General and a press release for use on Dominion Day, were sent by courier service on June 30 at a cost of $5,935. Even Santa Claus and his reindeer starting on June 30 could not get the packages throughout Canada by the next day, which was a holiday in any event. Certainly it would not be possible for any courier to do it, but they still spent $5,935.
If they had to be sent, why were they not sent by Canada Post? They arrived late anyway, so wasting $5,935 is inexcusable. No private company or business could stay in business if it wasted money in that manner.
Then comes the question, why were they sent at all? The weekly newspapers certainly did not ask for them, nor could they use such large maps in their weeklies. It appears that the photograph was really the important item. If it were used, it would enhance the Minister's vanity at the taxpayers' expense, of course, but it would do nothing else. What was this worth? Was it worth $3,000 of taxpayers' money?
There is another aspect to the answer of the Hon. Minister to the questions asked by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) regarding the cost of producing the package. The return tabled in the House of Commons indicated that the production cost was $1,783.08. On Monday night the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin stated that representatives of Energy, Mines and Resources told him that the price of the three maps was $5.95 and that no reduction was given. Therefore, the cost of the three maps is 576 times $5.95 or $3,427.20. Also last Monday the Parliamentary Secretary when replying to the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin stated:
The approximate cost of this was $3,000.
This was $3,000 for the photograph, approximately. Adding the cost of $3,000 for the photograph, to the $3,427.20 for the maps and the $1,783.08 for whatever the Minister included, the total is $8,210.28. But the Minister's return indicated that the production cost of the package was only $1,783.08. Does the total production cost not include the cost of the maps, the cost of the photograph, the cost of the fancy envelope, the cost of the two-page press release, etc.? Of course it does.
November 18, 1982

The tradition throughout British Parliaments is that Ministers must answer questions accurately. If such were not the case, there would be no use in Members of Parliament asking questions. I am asking the Government to investigate fully the answer which was tabled in the House by the Minister. If it was inaccurate-and I believe it was-the Minister should be asked for her resignation pronto. Otherwise it will be a mockery of Parliament. Parliament cannot operate unless truthful answers containing the whole truth are given by Ministers.
Also on Monday night the Parliamentary Secretary told how wonderful the maps were and are. No one is or was questioning the value of the maps. Of course they are splendid maps. We are questioning the extravagance of the Minister in a time of restraint and the inaccuracies contained in the reply tabled in the House. If the Minister wanted to be Santa Claus with the people's money and send out presents, she could have sent the maps to the weeklies via Canada Post, free; she could have sent them to the schools of Canada which would be far more sensible, free; or she could have sent them to the libraries of Canada, free, where they would have been used.
The total cost of the package plus the courier service appears to be in the vicinity of $10,000. It is almost a complete waste of money. No wonder the editor, a very knowledgeable lady, of the Cochrane Times, a weekly newspaper in Alberta, wrote a story which appeared on the front page on July 14, which ended with the question, "This is restraint?"
If the Minister had X dollars which she just had to spend, rather than waste it on this silly exercise that benefited largely only the courier, she could have spent it in a number of other ways. Here are a few suggested ways the Minister could have spent the money. She could have helped the unemployed in her own constituency and elsewhere who have used up their unemployment insurance benefits. They could stand a few cents to help them out. She could have given the money to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) so that he would not have to cut the indexing of the pensions of the superannuates, including retired RCMP and Armed Forces personnel and retired civil servants who actually paid for the indexing. What about the old age pensioners about whom we were talking tonight? The Minister could have given the money to the Salvation Army or to the Catholic Women's League to help them feed and clothe the poor and the unfortunate who tonight are cold, and many hungry. The Minister could have used the money to reduce the deficit or to lower the myriad of taxes which this money-hungry Government is imposing on the people, etc. etc. But, instead the Minister hired a courier at a cost to the taxpayer of $5,935 and sent out 576 photographs of herself at a cost of $3,000, as her parliamentary secretary revealed, to say nothing of the other costs.
Then to cinch the ridiculous, the Minister blatantly told the House:
Adjournment Debate
The cost of distribution is completely justified in the national interest.
This is a proper case for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) to investigate fully, and to make the findings public.

Mr. Speaker, I have examined the question asked by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) concerning the distribution of maps illustrating our country's growth to Canadian community newspapers so they would be able to use them during Canada Week. 1 am convinced that the public funds used for that purpose were a justifiable expenditure at a time when all Canadians were celebrating the achievements of their nation. The maps and the literature were sent to the newspapers in smaller communities so as to enable them to use those documents during Canada Week. In answer to a similar question earlier this week, it was clearly stated that those maps which depict the territorial evolution of Canada had a very particular meaning after we adopted our Constitution.
Because we wanted to have those maps widely known to the public, we decided to inform smaller towns and villages to the same extent as the larger urban communities which are already well served by the information networks. We had to use courier services to distribute the maps along with a photograph commemorating their presentation to His Excellency the Governor General so that Canadian Community Newspaper Association members would receive them before Canada Week, if at all possible. Originally, Canada Post was to look after the distribution of the maps, but unforeseen difficulties cropped up during the preparation, printing and wrapping of the maps and therefore they were not ready for distribution until late in June. Thanks to a courier service, it was however possible to deliver the material in time to allow its recipients to use it and give it the attention it deserved during Canada Week. Of course, as stated by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) a certain number of newspapers may not have received the material before Canada Day, July 1. However, I am pleased to know that thanks to the efforts which were made, they were able to use it as reference in the preparation of their forthcoming issues.
The printing of the maps did cost $1,783,08, as previously mentioned. The Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin said that the maps had cost $3,427.00 but he was referring to the retail price of the kit. subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PENSION RECOMMENDATION MADE BY UNITED VETERANS ORGANIZATION. (B) INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PENSION RECOMMENDATION MADE BY UNITED VETERANS ORGANIZATION. (B) INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
On November 2, 1982, I asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) the following question:
In June of this year the Minister said that he was giving very active consideration to the recommendation made by the United Veterans Organization which would ensure that veterans' pension increases would reflect the greater of the C.P.I. or the average increase given to the five lowest categories of civil servants. When is the Minister going to present the necessary legislative changes to Section 58 of the Pension Act so that veterans will be spared the task of going cap-in-hand to the Government for their annual increases?
The Minister was totally non-committal in his answer.
I also asked:
-has the Minister had any discussions with the Government House Leader as to when he can fit this veterans' legislation into our schedule for this year? It would be appropriate if we dealt with it this year. It is not a contentious issue. All that is required is one speaker from each Party. Has the Minister had any discussions with the Government House Leader?
The answer I received was no.
This question was preceded by a query respecting the method of calculating and making pension payments to veterans. Here again, 1 received a non-committal answer indicating the Government is not willing to bring in much needed legislation.
Legislation should be introduced before this session expires. The problem areas are numerous and, contrary to the Minister's belief that everything is operating smoothly, there are many recommendations made by veterans' organizations and the Official Opposition which have yet to be acted upon. Let me outline just a few to refresh our memories: A complete review of those recommendations made by the Woods Committee that have not yet been implemented; A complete review of all those recommendations made by the Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science Report entitled "They Serve, We care", which have not been implemented.
In this case special attention should be given to the apparent inequity of the way in which pension increases do not reflect the principle of parity with the average wage of five unskilled categories of public servants, or the increase in the consumer price index, whichever is greater, and that this principle is not entrenched in the Pension Act; the apparent inequity of the way in which veterans are compensated for periods spent as prisoners of war; and the increasing of the annual exemption for income derived from bank deposits, bonds and dividends to a minimum of $500. As well, there are recommendations aimed at having the Canada Pension Commission, the Entitlement Board and the Pension Review Board establish specific deadlines for each stage of the veterans pension application process. Finally, there are ways and means of increasing the use of the aging veterans' programs so that more veterans could take advantage of the system.
There are ongoing problems with the aging veterans' programs, even though the Minister has so much praise for it. The
details of the program are still not clear to local councillors, both in the application and implementation process.
There should be a review of current benefit payments for medical expenses in order to determine the feasibility of extending medical requirements currently provided for WVA-CWA recipients to spouses and eligible dependent children. Attention should be given to problems which the Indian War Veterans across Canada face in their attempt to receive their due benefits. The ongoing announcements concerning benefits to "new theatre of war" veterans should be formalized in legislation. Also, the question arising from the treatment of Hong Kong veterans and others with strongyloides should be intensified and increased in proficiency with the addition of mandatory tropical disease courses and training.
These are but a few of the main problem areas which must be addressed either through formal legislation or through programs debated and approved by the Veterans Affairs Committee. When the Veterans Affairs Committee met last June 1 presented a non-political motion calling on the Committee to work together constructively. Solutions could have been suggested by the elected representatives who are paid to work toward solutions in the first place. Had my motion passed, the Committee could have met regularly to receive progress reports from the Minister of Veterans Affairs on the many issues facing Canadian veterans. Unfortunately, the Liberal majority on the Committee voted down my motion, even though many like it have been passed by other committees in the past. This is truly a shame, since the committee will not meet again until the 1983-84 estimates are ready for study.
I was not expressing in my motion a lack of confidence in the Department's ability to solve problems. I was expressing my desire to have the elected representatives, who are supposed to be interested in helping formulate solutions to problems, work toward that goal in a non-partisan way. Unfortunately, the Liberal Members on the Committee did not envisage their role as elected representatives in the same way as I did.
When asked about upcoming legislation the Minister had no answers. When asked if he had even discussed the legislative timetable with the Government House Leader, the answer was no. Veterans do not deserve an irresponsible attitude such as this in light of the many areas of concern that still exist.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PENSION RECOMMENDATION MADE BY UNITED VETERANS ORGANIZATION. (B) INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to the Hon. Member's question. He referred to recommendations made in June of this year by the United Veterans Organizations, that the basic rate of pension be tied permanently to the greater of the composite average income of the five selected categories of public servants, or the Consumer Price Index. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) assured the Veterans Associations and this House that the recommendation is presently under consideration.
November 18, 1982

In 1972, this Government proposed and Parliament approved that there be an annual automatic adjustment in accordance with Consumer Price Index changes. That this has worked to the great benefit of these pensioners goes without saying.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, as a result of a study presided over by the Chairman of the Canadian Pension Commission, in which there was full and active participation of the veterans organizations, a new basis of establishing the basic rate of pension was arrived at. As a result, the basic rate of pension was substantially increased in 1973.
The formula which was introduced at that time related the pension paid to a 100 per cent disability pensioner, who was unmarried, to the composite average income of five selected categories of unskilled public servants, after income tax is paid at the rate in effect in the Province with the lowest rate. As you know, income tax is not payable on these pensions.
The single 100 per cent pensioner was better off than his composite counterpart in the Public Service until April 1, 1982, when several of the selected categories of public servants had wage adjustments. The basic rate will again be in favour of the 100 per cent unmarried pensioner after January 1, 1983, when the basic rate of pension is increased in accordance with the formula contained in the Pension Act. Eighty per cent of the disability pensioners are married and, therefore, most pensioners at present receive substantially more than the composite public servant who receives nothing extra for being married. Each year, all those in receipt of benefits under the Pension Act are compensated for any increases in the cost of living.
As Hon. Members are aware, the salaries of the selected categories of public servants have already been limited by legislation to increases of 6 per cent and 5 per cent within the next two years. Pensioners, on the other hand, will receive the full benefit of changes in the Consumer Price Index. This should result in a comparatively higher monthly rate. It is obvious that the yearly indexation as presently provided for by the Pension Act is more beneficial than trying to maintain parity with a selected group of public servants.

subtopic: NEW EMPLOYMENT EXPANSION AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM-TIMING OF FUND EXPENDITURES. (B) EXPENDITURES IN QUEBEC
NEW EMPLOYMENT EXPANSION AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM-TIMING OF FUND EXPENDITURES. (B) EXPENDITURES IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 16 of this year I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) a question in this House with regard to the new employment expansion and development Program, the centrepiece of the employment program and the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I found the Minister's response at that time totally inadequate. That is why I am rising again tonight to put the question; to make it clear so the Government can understand just what the question was. I would hope for a better response this evening.
The reason I rose to ask the question with regard to the NEED program is that in the Minister of Finance's economic
Adjournment Debate
statement he had claimed that this Program would operate over a period of 18 months, and in that period of 18 months it would create some 60,000 jobs.
We already knew that that description of the Program was an exaggeration, because labour analysts have indicated that as a rule of thumb, with $500 million you can create some
25.000	full-time jobs. When the Government says it will create
60.000	jobs for $500 million, obviously it is not talking about fulltime, full-year jobs, but part-time employment.
Our suspicions with regard to the NEED program were confirmed when the Minister held a press conference. In response to specific questions from the press, he had to admit he was talking about jobs that average between 20 and 30 weeks, which make them short-term jobs. Therefore, the program was being oversold.
I rose the other day because we on this side had learned from the provinces that the Minister was meeting with the provincial ministers of employment, indicating to them that this money was going to be spread over three fiscal years rather than over 18 months. 1 asked the Minister to confirm this. Whether the program lasts for a year and a half, two and a half years or three years is important, as it relates to the number of people who will get jobs and the amount of need this program will fill.
The Minister in a complicated way confirmed that the NEED program will run over three fiscal years and last some two and a half years. Therefore, we are talking about 30 months rather than the 18 months which the Minister of Finance indicated in his economic statement.
The Minister failed to acknowledge or give significance to the fact that the program would last much longer than announced by the Minister of Finance. It is important to acknowledge that if the program runs for 30 rather than 18 months, we will require more than $500 million to accomplish the purposes the Minister said would be accomplished; that is, to provide jobs for people who exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits. The Minister failed to recognize that. Therefore, he has failed in terms of taking greater action to meet the needs of those who run out of unemployment insurance benefits.
In my supplementary question I asked the Minister to acknowledge that under the program some $10 million would be spent in the Province of Quebec which has 23 per cent of its population on welfare or on unemployment insurance. The Minister failed to acknowledge this. He spoke about other figures, diverted attention, but did not deal with the seriousness of the unemployment situation in Quebec and the inadequacy of the Government's employment program as announced by the Minister of Finance.
I am very disappointed with the response of the Minister. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will deal more adequately tonight with the fact that rather than the program lasting for

18 months, it will in fact go for two and a half years. How does he expect a program that is already stretched to its limits to serve people for two and a half years rather than a year and a half? Does he expect people to believe that it will meet the needs of those who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits? The same amount of money that was originally announced for a year and a half will now be spent over two and a half years. Why is there this discrepancy between what was said in the economic statement of the Minister of Finance and what is actually happening?

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: NEW EMPLOYMENT EXPANSION AND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM-TIMING OF FUND EXPENDITURES. (B) EXPENDITURES IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to use the few minutes available to me to explain in clear terms the situation concerning job-creation programs. I believe that one must make a very clear distinction between existing job-creation programs under what we call the Community Development Program and the new job-creation program which we have called NEED. We now have in operation a Community Development Program through which unemployed workers can find a job anywhere in the country. These jobs will be created immediately under the existing program until the spring of 1983. This program will create approximately
25,000	jobs throughout the country.
As far as the NEED Program is concerned, one must make a very clear distinction and know what it is all about. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) were indeed right to speak of an 18-month program, and if we think of three fiscal years and use a little arithmetic, we indeed come to a figure of 18 months. Obviously, those are temporary jobs to
meet the very difficult situation which now exists in Canada. We shall provide temporary jobs for Canadians who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits or who will have completed their last 13 weeks.
We are speaking about $500 million to create 60,000 jobs. Obviously, if we were speaking about creating jobs for a one-year period, we would create fewer jobs, but if we provide employment for 12, 20 or 25 weeks, there will be more jobs. In quoting his figures, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) stated that labour experts were predicting the creation of fewer jobs, but let us look at the program announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and at the criteria given to us. The figure of 18 months has been mentioned and people are trying to say that the program will extend over two and a half years, but let us look at the figures, Mr. Speaker. We say 18 months and the program will come into effect on January 1, 1983. Therefore, there will be three months during the fiscal year 1982-83, then 12 months in the fiscal year 1983-84 and three months in 1984-85. This gives a total of 18 months for three fiscal years. Whatever way you look at it or add it up, the answer is the same and this money will help create jobs. In Quebec, we shall actually spend $10 million during the first three months, but over the 18-month period, we shall be spending $170 million. 1 hope this explanation will clarify the situation. What we want to do is to create
60,000	jobs throughout the country during the next 18 months.
